docs.title: Talk to ATC. It talks back.
docs.text:
Hold push-to-talk and speak as you would on a real radio. A controller answers in US FAA phraseology, on the frequency you are tuned to, from the gate at one airport to the gate at the next.

Get started What ATC can do

YouSeattle Clearance, November 547 Golf Alpha, IFR to Portland with Charlie.

ClearanceN547GA, cleared to Portland International airport via the SUMMA2 departure, then as filed. Climb and maintain 5000, expect 16000 10 minutes after departure. Departure frequency 119.2, squawk 4521.

YouCleared to Portland, SUMMA2 then as filed, 5000 expect 16000, 119.2, squawk 4521, 547GA. ✓ Readback accepted

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Every position talks to you

    Clearance Delivery, Ground, Tower, Departure, Center and Approach, each on its real frequency. Tune a frequency nobody is on and you hear nothing. At a field with no radio way to Clearance, you pick up the phone.

    What ATC can do

  • Real procedures

    IFR clearances, taxi routes with hold shorts, SIDs and STARs, climbs and descents, vectors to an ILS, RNAV or visual approach, and handoffs in between.

    A flight, gate to gate

  • Readbacks are checked

    A correct readback gets silence and a check mark. A wrong one is corrected: "negative, squawk six six six two".

    Readbacks

  • ATC calls you first

    Handoffs, a readback you forgot, an altitude you drifted from, traffic, a go-around: the controller speaks when a real one would.

    At every position

  • ATC's plan, drawn

    When Approach vectors you, the window draws the whole plan: the downwind, the base turn, where you join the final, and you.

    The approach plan

  • Any US airport

    Procedures, frequencies and airspace from the FAA's own data. Taxiways and parking from your own X-Plane scenery.

    Your X-Plane's data

  • Other aircraft in the sky

    Choose a Traffic level on New flight and AI aircraft depart, cross runways and land around you. ATC sequences you with them, and you can choose to hear their calls. In the client's 0.20 prereleases only, and for testers for now.

    AI traffic

  • Send your plan from ForeFlight

    Share the flight plan file to your account from your iPhone or the pilot site, then load it in the client with New flight, From my account (client 0.20 prerelease).

    Send a plan to your account

docs.title: What a flight is like
docs.text:
1. Start X-Plane 12 and the client. Press New flight and enter your flight plan, load it from SimBrief, or use a plan you sent to your account.
  2. Tune the ATIS and listen. Then call Clearance Delivery, get your clearance and read it back.
  3. Ground taxis you to the runway. Tower clears you for takeoff. Departure climbs you and puts you on course. Center takes you to cruise and brings you down again.
  4. Approach vectors you to final and clears the approach. Tower clears you to land and tells you where to leave the runway. Ground taxis you to the parking you ask for.

Your first flight walks through it step by step.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• X-Plane 12 on Windows, Linux or a Mac

    X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer, Windows 10 or 11, a 64-bit Linux desktop or an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 14 or newer (the Linux and Mac apps are prereleases for now), a microphone, and an internet connection during the flight. The controller runs in the cloud; the window beside X-Plane is a thin client.

  • An invitation

    SeventyOneTen is an invitation-only experiment. The owner creates your account; you download the installer from the pilot site (app.7110atc.com) once you are signed in. The product's home is 7110atc.com.

    Install and sign in · Linux · Mac

docs.title: Know before you fly
docs.text:
A simulation, and an experiment

SeventyOneTen is for flight simulation only. It must never be used for real-world flying, flight instruction or navigation. It is not an approved flight training device. It is under active development: what a controller says and does changes between releases, and things break.

  • IFR only, for now. VFR departures, pattern work and flight following are not built. A touch-and-go, stop-and-go or low approach is cleared when you ask for it.
  • US airports work best: everything outside the taxiways comes from the FAA's data. Outside the US, ATC asks your X-Plane for the airport's procedures and frequencies instead.
  • English, FAA phraseology.
  • When ATC is asked for something it has not been taught, it says so: "unable, I have not completed that training." It does not make something up.

All the known limitations are on one page.

docs.title: Your first flight
docs.text: An IFR flight from Seattle to Portland, gate to gate. The frequencies and names are examples: the window's Frequencies card lists the real ones for your flight.

docs.title: Before you call anyone
docs.text:
1. Start X-Plane 12 and put your aircraft on a stand at the departure airport.
  2. Start the client and wait for the startup dialog to close (signed in, ATC service ready).
  3. Press New flight.
    • Enter manually: tail number, aircraft type, departure, destination, cruise altitude and route. The dialog remembers your last plan. To fly as an airline, switch Tail number to Callsign and give the Airline (three letters), its Pronunciation (the word ATC says, filled in for the airlines the client knows) and the Flight number. A line under the fields says what ATC will say, such as "Walker seventeen forty-five", and the window's header shows "Walker 1745".
    • From SimBrief: enter your SimBrief username or pilot ID and press Load. It fills in your latest flight plan and tells you which one it loaded and how old it is. No password or key is needed.
    • From my account (client 0.20 prerelease): the newest plan you sent to your account from ForeFlight or another app. Press Use this plan to fill in the form, then check it.
    • Traffic (client 0.20 prerelease): None is the default. Choose a level and AI aircraft fly around you: see AI traffic.
  4. Press Start flight. The dialog says Starting new flight… and closes when ATC is ready (with Traffic on, when the traffic is drawn: see AI traffic).

The client also writes your plan for X-Plane's own avionics (client 0.20 prerelease), so you can load it into the GNS 530, the G1000 or the FMS. Your plan in X-Plane's avionics says how.

The first flight after installing takes longer

The first time, the client reads the headers of your X-Plane scenery once, so it can answer ATC's questions about taxiways and parking. The dialog shows a progress bar. On a slow disk this can take a minute or more. After that, only new or updated scenery is read.

docs.title: How to talk
docs.text:
• Push-to-talk: hold the big button in the window, hold Space while the window has focus, or use a yoke or joystick button (Settings).
  • You transmit on the COM radio selected on your aircraft's audio panel, on its active frequency. The push-to-talk button names who is listening there.
  • Say who you are calling, your callsign, and what you want, as on a real radio. Read back clearances and instructions.
  • You hear ATC only if COM1 or COM2 is tuned to the frequency ATC transmits on, is switched on, and is selected to listen on your audio panel. A radio that is off, or not selected to listen, is silent, and you cannot transmit on it.
  • While X-Plane is paused, ATC is silent and does not hear you.

docs.title: 1. ATIS
docs.text: Tune the ATIS frequency on either radio. The recording loops, starting mid-broadcast like the real thing. Note the information letter and the altimeter.

docs.title: 2. Clearance Delivery
docs.text:
You: Seattle Clearance, November five four seven Golf Alpha, IFR to Portland with information Charlie.

ATC: November five four seven Golf Alpha, cleared to Portland International airport via the Summa Two departure, then as filed, climb and maintain five thousand, expect one six thousand ten minutes after departure, departure frequency one one niner point two, squawk four five two one.

You: Cleared to Portland, Summa Two then as filed, five thousand expect one six thousand, one one niner point two, squawk four five two one, five four seven Golf Alpha.

ATC: November five four seven Golf Alpha, readback correct.

Prefer not to copy a clearance by voice? Request a PDC and it arrives as text.

docs.title: 3. Ground
docs.text:
You: Seattle Ground, November five four seven Golf Alpha, at alpha eleven, ready to taxi with Charlie.

Ground gives you a route along your scenery's real taxiways, with a hold short for each runway on the way. Read back the runway and each hold short for a crossing. Ask for a pushback first if you need one. If you get lost, say "request progressive taxi" and Ground calls each turn as you come up to it.

docs.title: 4. Tower
docs.text: At the hold line, the window shows Next: Seattle Tower with buttons that put the frequency in a radio's standby. Call ready. Tower may line you up and wait, hold you for traffic or wake turbulence, or clear you for takeoff with the runway, the wind and your initial heading.

docs.title: 5. Departure and Center
docs.text:
Once you are airborne and half a mile from the runway, Tower hands you to Departure (at 1,000 ft above the ground at the latest). Check in with your altitude:

You: Seattle Departure, November five four seven Golf Alpha, one thousand two hundred climbing five thousand.

Departure says "radar contact", climbs you and turns you on course. Center takes over on the way up and, later, starts your descent: "descend via the Helns Six arrival", or a crossing restriction. Along the way you can ask for another altitude, direct to a fix on your route, or a deviation around weather.

docs.title: 6. Approach
docs.text:
Approach tells you which approach to expect and vectors you to final. The first vector says why: "..., vectors for the ILS runway one zero right". ATC does not say the pattern it plans: the window's Approach card draws it, and the top line of the window confirms that ATC is vectoring you.

ATC: November five four seven Golf Alpha, turn left heading one three zero, maintain three thousand until established, cleared ILS runway one zero right approach.

Read back the heading, the altitude and the approach with its runway. Approach then hands you to Tower.

docs.title: 7. Tower, landing and taxi-in
docs.text: Tower clears you to land with the wind. Read back "cleared to land" with the runway. Where it matters, Tower tells you on the rollout where to turn off; either way it hands you to Ground. Tell Ground where you are parking: a gate, an FBO, or "general aviation". If ATC asks "say parking", the window's Parking card lists the names you can say and shows them on a map. It also comes up on its own when you land and slow to 30 kt or less, and when you switch to Ground.

docs.title: 8. The end of the flight
docs.text: Park at your stand and shut down the engines. The flight ends by itself within about a minute. You can also press End flight, and closing X-Plane ends the flight after 30 seconds.

docs.title: If something goes wrong
docs.text:
• Silence after you transmit? The log's No reply line says why. See Troubleshooting.
  • Missed what ATC said? Say "say again". The words are also in the log. If ATC called while your radio was off or not selected to listen, it says that call again once the radio can hear it, within about a minute.
  • Closed the client mid-flight by accident? Start it again within about ten minutes and choose Rejoin last flight.

docs.title: Install and sign in
docs.text: SeventyOneTen has two parts. The controller runs in the cloud. On your sim PC you run a small program, the client, in its own window beside X-Plane. It reads your aircraft's state from X-Plane, sends your voice while you hold push-to-talk, and plays ATC's replies through a radio effect.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Simulator X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer. The client uses X-Plane's own Web API, and needs the version of it that arrived in 12.1.4. Tested on 12.4.3. Use the current X-Plane 12 release PC Windows 10 or 11. The window uses Edge WebView2, which ships with both. On Linux, see Install on Linux. On an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 14 or newer, see Install on a Mac Audio A microphone, and speakers or a headset Account A SeventyOneTen account, created for you by the project owner The client The installer (Windows), the AppImage (Linux) or the disk image (Mac), from the pilot site once you are signed in (below) Phone An authenticator app, for the sign-in's second step

Invitation only

SeventyOneTen is an experiment and is not open for sign-up. If you were invited, the owner has sent you an email with a temporary password.

docs.title: Install (one time)
docs.text:
These steps are for Windows. On Linux, follow Install on Linux; on a Mac, follow Install on a Mac. Then come back here to sign in.

  1. Go to the pilot site, app.7110atc.com, and sign in with your SeventyOneTen account. Open Download (https://app.7110atc.com/#/download) and press Download for Windows. The file is xatc-agent-setup-<version>.exe.
  2. Run it. It installs for your Windows account only and does not ask for an administrator password.
  3. The installer is not signed yet, so Windows may say "Windows protected your PC". Choose More info, then Run anyway. Do this only for a file you downloaded from the Download page while signed in.
  4. Open SeventyOneTen from the Start menu (or from the last page of the installer).
  5. Allow the microphone: Windows Settings > Privacy & security > Microphone > Let desktop apps access your microphone.

There is nothing else to install and no keys to copy. You sign in from the window.

Installed it before 20 October 2026? Reinstall once, by hand

On 2026-10-20 the pilot site moved to app.7110atc.com (the product's home is 7110atc.com). A client older than 0.20.0-rc.11 looks for updates at the old address, so it can no longer find them: download the newest installer from app.7110atc.com/#/download and run it over your copy. After that, updates arrive by themselves again.

The installed app updates itself: see Updates. To remove it, use Windows Settings > Apps > SeventyOneTen > Uninstall. Your settings and log stay in %LOCALAPPDATA%\xatc-agent-client until you delete that folder. Your sign-in stays in Windows Credential Manager until you press Sign out in the window; do that before uninstalling if you want it gone.

docs.title: Start the client
docs.text:
Open SeventyOneTen from the Start menu. The SeventyOneTen client window opens with the startup dialog: one row each for your sign-in, the ATC service and X-Plane. There is no console window; the log file holds what a console would show.

  • X-Plane is shown but not required yet. Start it whenever you like; the client keeps looking for it.
  • Only one client runs at a time. Starting it again brings the window that is already open to the front.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
1. Press Sign in in the startup dialog. Your browser opens the SeventyOneTen sign-in page.
  2. The first time, enter your email and the temporary password from your invitation, choose your own password, and set up your authenticator app. After that it is your email, your password and the authenticator's code (or a passkey, if you add one). Passkeys must be added again after the sign-in move of 2026-10-20: a passkey belongs to the sign-in address, so the old ones no longer work. Sign in with your password and the authenticator's code, then add the passkey again.
  3. The browser says Signed in and you can close the tab. The window's sign-in pill turns green.

You stay signed in for 30 days, across restarts. In the last 24 hours the window offers Sign in again, which never interrupts a flight. The client keeps your sign-in in Windows Credential Manager (on a Mac, in your Keychain; on Linux, in your keyring), never in a file.

docs.title: Choose your audio
docs.text:
ATC's address comes with your account. When you sign in, the client gets it. Under Your account, Settings has an ATC part with one line about it: From your account. once the client has it.

  1. Open the Settings view (the startup dialog closes by itself once you are signed in).
  2. Under Your setup > Audio, pick your microphone and your speakers or headset.
  3. Press Save, at the bottom of the page.

If the ATC line says the address could not be fetched, press Try again.

That is all the setup. Settings describes everything else you can change, such as push-to-talk on a yoke button (Your setup) and how the controllers sound (How ATC sounds).

docs.title: The recording question
docs.text:
The first time you connect, the window asks one thing before you can transmit:

Keep your radio audio to improve SeventyOneTen? SeventyOneTen can keep recordings of what you say on the radio, to help it understand pilots better. Only your own transmissions are kept, in private storage, for 180 days. The owner and the ATC expert can listen to them. SeventyOneTen also keeps the text its speech recognizer wrote down for what you said, with your flight's record, for as long as that flight is kept: only the audio is deleted after 180 days. You can change this at any time in Settings. Your flight's transcript is always kept with the flight. The recording and the recognizer's own text are kept only if you allow it.

Choose Allow or Don't allow. Your choice is remembered with your account, and you can change it in Settings > Your account > Recording. Your data says what else is sent and kept.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Two parts: a thin client on your sim PC, and the controller in the cloud. One encrypted connection joins them for the whole flight.

How the parts of SeventyOneTen work together On your PC, X-Plane 12 gives the SeventyOneTen client the aircraft's state, and the client tunes X-Plane's radios; your microphone and headset carry your voice in and ATC's audio out. The client signs in through your browser with the sign-in service, then keeps one encrypted connection per flight to the ATC service in the cloud. It sends the aircraft's state, your voice and answers about your scenery, and receives ATC's audio and text, the approach plan and parking. In the ATC service, speech recognition hears the call, an AI model understands it, the controller agent (an AI model) decides which ATC tool to use, the tool checks the request and writes the phraseology, and text to speech speaks it. Monitors watch every frame and start ATC's own calls through the same tools. The tools read the FAA's data. Each flight is written to a flight log that is reviewed afterwards. Your PC The cloud X-Plane 12 your aircraft, weather, traffic, scenery SeventyOneTen client push-to-talk, radios, the cards plays ATC through a radio effect Microphone and headset aircraft state radio tuning your voice ATC audio Sign-in service knows which pilot is flying sign in, in your browser aircraft state your voice, while you hold push-to-talk answers about your scenery, when asked one encrypted connection per flight ATC's audio and text the approach plan parking, frequencies ATC service one isolated session per flight Hear speech to text Understand reads the call Decide picks a tool ATC tools check, phrase Speak text to speech Monitors watch every frame, call you first ATC's own calls A readback is judged by the AI model, item by item; code checks every quote against what you said. The FAA's data procedures, frequencies, airspace, altitudes Flight log reviewed after an AI model plain code: it checks, and it writes ATC's words data How the parts work together. The AI model understands and chooses; plain code checks the request and writes what ATC says.

docs.title: One radio call
docs.text:
1. You key the mic. The client streams your audio while push-to-talk is held, beside a frame of aircraft state about once a second.
  2. Speech recognition turns the audio into text. It is tuned for aviation phraseology, and with the Scribe choice in Settings it is also given the names from your flight (callsign, cities, procedures, route fixes).
  3. Plain code checks the basics: is a controller on that frequency, and did your callsign come through.
  4. An AI model reads the call. Is it a readback of what ATC just said, a request, or both?
  5. A readback is judged item by item, quoting your own words. Code refuses any quote that is not in the transcript, then decides: accept in silence, correct one item, or ask once for a safety item.
  6. A request goes to the controller agent, an AI model that plays the position you called. Its job is to pick the right tool for what you asked: issue a taxi clearance, assign an altitude, clear an approach.
  7. The tool does the controlling. It checks the request against the FAA's data, your scenery and the state of your flight, writes the exact phraseology, and refuses in fixed words when the data says no.
  8. Text to speech speaks it, the client adds the radio effect (the optional radio voices already sound like a radio, so they get only the key-up click), and you hear it if a radio that is on and selected to listen is tuned to that frequency. A call you could not hear is said again once when the radio can hear it, within about a minute.

Meanwhile monitors watch every frame of your aircraft's state and start ATC's own calls: handoffs, readback reminders, an altitude that drifted, traffic.

docs.title: Where the AI is, and where it is not
docs.text:
The AI model understands what you said and chooses what kind of thing a controller would do next. It does not invent the clearance.

The model does Code does Classifies your transmission Decides whether a controller is listening on that frequency Judges a readback against what was said Checks that every quoted word was really in your transmission Picks the tool for your request Checks the request against the data: runways, procedures, minimum altitudes, traffic Writes the words ATC speaks, in standard phraseology Watches your flight and starts ATC's own calls

A model can still pick the wrong tool. When it does, the tool refuses rather than issue something the data does not support, and the cost is a retry or an "unable", not a wrong clearance. When no tool fits, ATC says "unable, I have not completed that training".

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
• The FAA's published data, updated every 28-day cycle: procedures (SIDs, STARs, approaches), fixes and airways, facility frequencies and hours, airspace boundaries, minimum vectoring and minimum IFR altitudes.
  • Your X-Plane, asked when needed: taxiways, stands and runway use. The weather and traffic around you are sent continuously. See Your X-Plane's data.

docs.title: One session per flight
docs.text: Each flight gets its own isolated session in the cloud, which keeps the flight's state: your clearance, where you are in the flight, what you still owe a readback for. It survives a reconnect (a transmission lost in a dropped connection is sent again once), and it stops when the flight ends.

docs.title: Why it takes a moment to answer
docs.text: Each reply involves speech recognition, two or three model calls (a router for every call, a judge for a readback, the controller agent for a request), and speech synthesis. Expect a few seconds from releasing push-to-talk to the first word. The log's Timing line shows each step.

docs.title: Install on Linux
docs.text:
The Linux client is an AppImage: one file that you download, make executable and run. There is nothing to install and no terminal is needed. It is for 64-bit Intel and AMD PCs (x86_64) only.

A prerelease, for now

The Linux app first came with client 0.20, which is a prerelease: a build for testing, not yet a stable release. The Download page shows it under Prerelease (with a warning that it can have faults), and when no Linux version has been published it says No Linux release yet. Install it if you have been asked to, or if you are happy to test. When a stable release carries it, this note goes.

The Linux app is new and has been run by fewer pilots than the Windows one. If something does not work, report it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Simulator X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer, as on every platform PC A 64-bit (x86_64) Linux desktop. The app is built on Ubuntu 22.04, so it also runs on Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 12, Fedora 38 and later, and Linux Mint 21 and later Window WebKit2GTK 4.1, from your system, so the app opens in its own window. Ubuntu 24.04 and most desktop distributions have it. Without it, the same panel opens in your web browser and works the same Staying signed in A keyring: GNOME Keyring or KWallet. Without one you sign in each time you start the app Audio A microphone, and speakers or a headset Account A SeventyOneTen account, created for you by the project owner Phone An authenticator app, for the sign-in's second step

docs.title: Install (one time)
docs.text:
1. Go to the pilot site, app.7110atc.com, and sign in with your SeventyOneTen account. Open Download, choose Linux (x86_64 AppImage), then press Download for Linux. The file is xatc-agent-<version>-x86_64.AppImage.
  2. Make it executable. Either:
    • in your file manager, open the file's Properties and tick Allow executing as program; or
    • in a terminal, run chmod +x xatc-agent-<version>-x86_64.AppImage.
  3. Run it by double-clicking it (or ./xatc-agent-<version>-x86_64.AppImage in a terminal). The SeventyOneTen client window opens.
  4. Allow the microphone if your desktop asks.

If the file will not start and the message mentions FUSE, run it in a terminal as APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN=1 ./xatc-agent-<version>-x86_64.AppImage.

The file is not signed. The Download page shows the file's SHA-256; to check that your copy is the one the page describes, run sha256sum xatc-agent-<version>-x86_64.AppImage and compare the result with the page. Download the file only from the Download page while signed in.

From here, sign in and choose your audio exactly as on Windows.

docs.title: Add the app to your app menu
docs.text:
The first time you run the AppImage, the window offers to add the app to your app menu: Add or Not now. Add gives you a menu entry and an icon, so you can start it like any other app. Settings > Your setup has the same thing, under App menu: Add to app menu, and Remove from app menu to undo it.

The menu entry points at the AppImage file where it is now. If you move the file, add the entry again from Settings > Your setup > App menu.

docs.title: Staying signed in
docs.text: You stay signed in for 30 days, across restarts, when your desktop has a keyring (GNOME Keyring or KWallet), which the app uses to keep your sign-in. The sign-in is never written to a file. Most desktop distributions set a keyring up for you. Without one, the app still works, but you sign in each time you start it.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
The app asks the pilot site for the newest version when it starts, and once a day while it is open. A newer version shows a banner: What changed, Update now and Later. The banner waits until your flight has ended, and nothing is installed during a flight.

Update now replaces the AppImage file with the new version, checks it first, and opens the app again by itself. Because it replaces the file, the AppImage must be somewhere you can write to, such as your home folder. Until Linux is in a stable release, newer Linux builds are prereleases, and the app offers a prerelease only when Receive prereleases is on in Settings > Your account > Updates: see Updates. If an update fails, your old file is left as it was and the banner says why.

docs.title: Where things are kept
docs.text:
What Where Settings ~/.config/xatc-agent-client/settings.json The log file ~/.config/xatc-agent-client/logs/xatc-agent-client.log Your sign-in Your keyring, under xatc-agent-client. Never in a file

To remove the app, delete the AppImage file and, if you added it, use Remove from app menu first. The settings folder stays until you delete it.

docs.title: Install on a Mac
docs.text:
The Mac app is a disk image: you download it, drag the app to your Applications folder and open it. There is nothing else to install and no terminal is needed. It is for Apple silicon Macs (M1 or later) running macOS 14 or newer.

A prerelease, for now

The Mac app came with client 0.20 (since 0.20.0-rc.10), which is a prerelease: a build for testing, not yet a stable release. The Download page shows it under Prerelease (with a warning that it can have faults). Install it if you have been asked to, or if you are happy to test. When a stable release carries it, this note goes.

The Mac app is new and has been run by fewer pilots than the Windows one. If something does not work, report it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Simulator X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer, as on every platform, running on the same Mac Mac An Apple silicon Mac (M1 or later) with macOS 14 or newer. There is no build for Intel Macs Audio A microphone, and speakers or a headset Account A SeventyOneTen account, created for you by the project owner Phone An authenticator app, for the sign-in's second step

docs.title: Install (one time)
docs.text:
1. Go to the pilot site, app.7110atc.com, and sign in with your SeventyOneTen account. Open Download, choose Mac (Apple silicon), then press Download for Mac under Prerelease. The file is xatc-agent-<version>-arm64.dmg.
  2. Open the downloaded .dmg file. A disk image named SeventyOneTen and the version opens, with the app and your Applications folder side by side.
  3. Drag xatc-agent to your Applications folder. Finder shows the app by its file name, xatc-agent; the window it opens is called SeventyOneTen client.
  4. Eject the disk image.
  5. Open xatc-agent from Applications, not from the disk image.
  6. The first time, macOS asks whether SeventyOneTen may use the microphone. Allow it, so the app can hear you.

If you said no by mistake, open System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone and switch on xatc-agent (it may be listed as SeventyOneTen).

From here, sign in and choose your audio exactly as on Windows.

docs.title: Is this the right file?
docs.text:
The app is signed with the project's Apple developer certificate and notarized by Apple, so macOS can check it. (The Windows installer and the Linux AppImage are not signed.) The Download page also shows the file's SHA-256. To check that your copy is the one the page describes, run this in Terminal and compare the result with the page:

shasum -a 256 xatc-agent-<version>-arm64.dmg

Download the file only from the Download page while signed in.

docs.title: Staying signed in
docs.text: You stay signed in for 30 days, across restarts. The app keeps your sign-in in your Mac's Keychain, under xatc-agent-client. It is never written to a file. Sign out in the window removes it.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
The app asks the pilot site for the newest version when it starts, and once a day while it is open. A newer version shows a banner: What changed, Update now and Later. The banner waits until your flight has ended, and nothing is installed during a flight.

Update now downloads the new version, checks that it is the release that was offered and that it is this app, replaces the app and opens it again by itself. If anything is wrong, your old app is left as it was and the banner says why.

Because it replaces the app, the app must be in Applications (or another folder you can write to). An app opened straight from the disk image, or left in Downloads, is not updated: move it to Applications first. Until the Mac app is in a stable release, newer Mac builds are prereleases, and the app offers a prerelease only when Receive prereleases is on in Settings > Your account > Updates: see Updates.

docs.title: Where things are kept
docs.text:
What Where Settings ~/Library/Application Support/xatc-agent-client/settings.json The log file ~/Library/Application Support/xatc-agent-client/logs/xatc-agent-client.log (Settings, at the bottom, has Open log folder, which opens it in Finder) The current flight, for Rejoin last flight ~/.xatc-agent/session.json Your sign-in Your Keychain, under xatc-agent-client. Never in a file

None of these is inside the app.

docs.title: Remove the app
docs.text: Drag xatc-agent from Applications to the Trash. Your settings, log and session file stay until you delete them. Your sign-in stays in your Keychain until you press Sign out in the window, so do that first if you want it gone.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Sign in, then your first flight.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
SeventyOneTen is an invitation-only experiment under active development. These are the edges as of 2026-10-28; each will be removed from this page when it is fixed.

  • IFR only. Every flight is an IFR flight. VFR departures, pattern work, flight following and VFR arrivals are not built.
  • The United States first. The FAA's data covers the US only. Elsewhere ATC works from your X-Plane's own navigation data for the airport's procedures, fixes and frequencies, and it has no airspace boundaries, Center sectors or minimum vectoring altitudes for the area, so expect less of it there. The project has not flown outside the US. See Your X-Plane's data.
  • Windows, Linux and Mac, and X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer. The client is a Windows 10 or 11 app. A Linux app for 64-bit (x86_64) PCs and a Mac app for Apple silicon Macs (macOS 14 or newer) exist as prereleases only, not yet in a stable release: see Install on Linux and Install on a Mac. There is no build for Intel Macs. The client talks to X-Plane through its own Web API. X-Plane has had that API since 12.1.1, and the client needs the version of it that arrived in 12.1.4. Laminar is still extending it release by release, so use the current X-Plane 12. Tested on 12.4.3. It does not work with X-Plane 11 or other simulators. With an older X-Plane 12 the client shows X-Plane: not connected: see X-Plane too old.
  • The X-Plane data pack replaces the FAA procedure file. ATC flies the FAA's procedures of the current cycle. Settings > X-Plane data can install them into X-Plane's Custom Data folder so your aircraft's FMS and ATC agree. While the pack is installed, X-Plane's own GPS shows the FAA's procedures too, and Remove puts your files back. See FAA procedures for your X-Plane.
  • Some requests are not built. A block altitude, a sidestep to a parallel runway, vectors to the nearest airport and lost-communication routings are not built. ATC answers "unable, I have not completed that training". For an emergency, the first steps are there ("say fuel remaining and souls on board", priority) and not much beyond them. See What ATC can do.
  • Some replies are still intermittent. In a small number of situations the controller answers correctly most of the time, but not every time. The list shrinks with each release.
  • Controller voices. All the voices are synthetic and speak American English; the radio voices add regional American accents. Settings > How ATC sounds has four choices for ATC voices: the radio voices, which give each controller a distinct voice and already sound like a radio, and three standard voices from the most robotic to the most natural. See Settings.
  • Fix names. ATC says a VOR by its name. It says a fix the way controllers say it where a real source confirms it, which so far is a few. Any other fix it says as written ("PANGL" as "Pangl") rather than guess. If a name sounds wrong to you, report it with the time.
  • The Windows and Linux downloads are not signed. When you run the Windows installer you downloaded, Windows says "Windows protected your PC". Choose More info, then Run anyway, for a file you downloaded from the pilot site's Download page while signed in. See Install. The Linux AppImage has no signature either: check its SHA-256 against the Download page, as Install on Linux describes. The Mac app is signed and notarized by Apple: see Install on a Mac.
  • Staying signed in on Linux needs a keyring. GNOME Keyring or KWallet keeps your sign-in between runs. Without one, you sign in each time you start the app.
  • One client per PC. Starting the client again brings the window that is already open to the front.

docs.title: If you hit something that is not here
docs.text: Say what you said, what you expected and the time, and send the log file: see Reporting a problem.

docs.title: Your data
docs.text: What the client sends, what is kept, and what stays on your PC. This page describes how the software works. It is not a legal agreement. SeventyOneTen is an invitation-only experiment; ask the project owner about anything this page does not answer.

docs.title: Your account
docs.text:
You sign in with a SeventyOneTen account that the owner creates for you: your email address, a password you choose, and an authenticator app or a passkey.

  • The client never sees your password. You type it into the sign-in page in your own browser.
  • The client keeps your sign-in in Windows Credential Manager (on a Mac, in your Keychain; on Linux, in your keyring), for up to 30 days. It is never written to a file.
  • ATC knows which account is flying. A flight belongs to the pilot who started it, and nobody else can rejoin it.
  • Sign out removes the sign-in from your PC and cancels it with the sign-in service.

docs.title: What the client sends during a flight
docs.text:
Over one encrypted connection to ATC, for as long as a flight is running:

What When Your flight plan: callsign, aircraft type, departure, destination, cruise altitude, route When the flight starts Your aircraft's state: position, altitude, speed, heading, radios (frequencies, and whether each is on and selected to listen), transponder code, on the ground or not About once a second The weather at your aircraft and X-Plane's clock Every few seconds The other aircraft in your X-Plane (the nearest 32), including AI traffic if you turned it on About once a second Your microphone Only while you hold push-to-talk. The exception is an experimental two-way phone call, where it is open for the whole call Answers to ATC's questions about your scenery: an airport's taxiways and stands When ATC asks. See Your X-Plane's data

No connection to ATC is open when no flight is running, and your microphone is never sent outside push-to-talk, except on a two-way phone call you chose.

docs.title: What happens to your voice
docs.text:
While you hold push-to-talk, your audio is streamed to a speech recognition service and turned into text. The text is what ATC works from.

When the client's Speech recognition setting is Scribe, the audio of your transmissions goes to a third-party speech service outside SeventyOneTen's own systems, to be written down. When it is Standard, or if that service cannot be reached, SeventyOneTen's own speech recognition writes it down within SeventyOneTen's systems.

The full statement, which names the services, is the Privacy page on the pilot site.

docs.title: Two-way phone calls (experimental)
docs.text: On a clearance call you can choose a Two-way call in Settings (Phone calls). It is experimental and offered only on some accounts. On a two-way call there is no push-to-talk button: your microphone is open for the whole call, and the call's audio goes to a live voice service that carries the conversation. With Two-way B that is a third-party service outside SeventyOneTen's own systems; the Privacy page on the pilot site names the services. SeventyOneTen does not keep the audio of a two-way call, whatever you chose in the recording question below. On Push to talk, the default, a call is like the radio: the microphone is open only while you hold the key.

docs.title: Recordings of your voice
docs.text:
By default nothing you say is kept as audio. The first time you connect, the window asks:

Keep your radio audio to improve SeventyOneTen? SeventyOneTen can keep recordings of what you say on the radio, to help it understand pilots better. Only your own transmissions are kept, in private storage, for 180 days. The owner and the ATC expert can listen to them. SeventyOneTen also keeps the text its speech recognizer wrote down for what you said, with your flight's record, for as long as that flight is kept: only the audio is deleted after 180 days. You can change this at any time in Settings. Your flight's transcript is always kept with the flight. The recording and the recognizer's own text are kept only if you allow it.

  • You must choose Allow or Don't allow before you can transmit.
  • The choice is stored with your account, so you are asked once, not once per PC.
  • Change it at any time in Settings > Your account > Recording.
  • When the wording of the question changes, every pilot is asked again. The wording above (version 3) first ships with the next client release (it reaches you first as a prerelease if you have opted in; see Settings for how prereleases are offered), so you will see the question once more after you update to a client that carries it; client 0.19.0 still shows the earlier wording.

docs.title: What is kept about a flight
docs.text:
Each flight is logged so that it can be reviewed and the controller improved:

  • what you said, as text, and what ATC answered,
  • what ATC decided,
  • your aircraft's track,
  • which account flew it.

The project owner, an air traffic control expert who advises the project, and the project's testers review flights in a private tool. They can see the items above. Only the owner and the expert can listen to your recordings, and only if you allowed them.

If you allowed recordings, the flight's record also keeps the text the speech recognizer wrote down for what you said, exactly as it wrote it, for as long as the flight is kept. That is longer than the audio: only the audio is deleted after 180 days; the text stays with the flight. If you chose Don't allow, that text is not kept (the transcript of what you said, listed above, always is). Text already kept with earlier flights stays with them.

A flight log is kept until it is deleted: there is no automatic expiry today. The pilot site's Privacy page says how to ask for a copy of what is held about you, or for your account, flights or recordings to be deleted.

docs.title: Plans you send to your account
docs.text: If you send a flight plan to your account, SeventyOneTen keeps your five most recent plans (the airports, route, altitude and tail number in each, and the file's name) so you can load one in the client. The file itself is not stored. Older plans are removed as new ones arrive, and all of them are deleted with your account. The iPhone app keeps its sign-in in the iPhone's Keychain and sends a file only when you tap Send.

docs.title: Other services
docs.text:
• The radio voices. ATC's voice is made by SeventyOneTen's own text to speech. Only when ATC voices is set to Radio voices do the words ATC says on the radio go instead, as text, to a third-party speech service outside SeventyOneTen's own systems, to give each controller a distinct voice and accent. Only ATC's words are sent, never your voice. The setting is off by default. Push-to-talk phone calls, the ATIS and AWOS are always spoken by SeventyOneTen's own text to speech, and so is any radio transmission that the third-party service cannot speak in time. On a two-way call the live voice service speaks ATC's words too (see Two-way phone calls).
  • The AI model. The text of your transmissions, with the facts of your flight, is processed by an AI model to work out what you asked for and to judge readbacks. See How it works.
  • SimBrief. If you load a flight plan from SimBrief, the client fetches your latest plan from SimBrief with the username or pilot ID you typed. No SimBrief password or key is involved.

docs.title: What stays on your PC
docs.text:
• Settings: ATC's address (written from your account's answer, never shown in the window, and recorded in the log file), your SimBrief username or pilot ID, your X-Plane folder, your last flight plan. No password and no key.
  • The log file: connections, ATC's address, what ATC asked of your X-Plane, warnings and errors. Never your sign-in and never audio.
  • The window answers only to your own PC. No website can press your push-to-talk, sign you in or sign you out.
  • Your X-Plane files are read, never uploaded as files. The client writes to your X-Plane folder in two places only: the optional FAA procedures, which you install and remove yourself, and your flight plan, the one file Output/FMS plans/SeventyOneTen.fms, which is written when you start a flight and never sent anywhere.

docs.title: Send a plan to your account
docs.text:
If you plan your flights in ForeFlight or another planning app, you do not have to type the plan into the client. Send the plan file to your SeventyOneTen account, from your iPhone or from the pilot site, then load it in the client with New flight > From my account.

A prerelease, for now

From my account is in the client's 0.20 prereleases (since 0.20.0-rc.10). The stable client, 0.19.0, does not have it. Sending a plan from the pilot site works for everyone with an account. The iPhone app is a test version for invited testers.

docs.title: What a plan file is
docs.text:
SeventyOneTen reads three kinds of file:

  • .fpl, the flight plan file that ForeFlight exports;
  • .gfp, a plain text plan;
  • .gpx, a GPX route file.

From the file it takes the departure, the destination, the route, the cruise altitude and the tail number. A flight of two airports with no fixes in between is a direct flight, and its route stays empty with no "missing" mark. A .fpl file can also carry an aircraft type, which the pilot site reads when it is there (ForeFlight's does not carry one). The file must be no larger than 256 KB.

docs.title: Send a plan from your iPhone
docs.text:
The iPhone app is called SeventyOneTen. It is available through TestFlight, Apple's test program, to testers the owner has invited.

  1. Open the app once and press Sign in. You sign in with your SeventyOneTen account, as in the client.
  2. In ForeFlight, open the flight, tap Share, and choose SeventyOneTen from the Share menu.
  3. A card shows the file. Nothing is sent until you tap Send. If the file is not a flight plan the card says so, and nothing is sent.

The app's home screen lists the plans you sent recently, and has Sign out.

docs.title: Send a plan from the pilot site
docs.text:
1. Sign in to the pilot site, app.7110atc.com, and open Send a plan (beside Download).
  2. In ForeFlight, open the flight, tap Share, then Save to Files. Then choose the file on the page. It is sent as soon as you choose it.
  3. The page shows what it found in the file, and says what is not in it. Anything the file lacks, you fill in when you start the flight.

Your recent plans on that page lists what you sent.

docs.title: Load the plan in the client
docs.text:
1. Press New flight, and choose the From my account tab.
  2. The tab shows your newest plan: the two airports, the route, the cruise altitude and the tail number, and when and from where it was sent, such as "Sent from your iPhone, 2 min ago".
  3. Press Use this plan. It fills in the flight plan for you to check. Anything the plan lacks is left empty and marked.
  4. Check the fields, then press Start flight.

The tail number from the plan fills only an empty Tail number field, so it never replaces a callsign you already entered. Starting the flight marks the plan as used.

If you are not signed in, the tab has a Sign in button. If the plan could not be fetched, it has Try again.

docs.title: What is kept
docs.text: SeventyOneTen keeps your five most recent plans: the airports, route, altitude and tail number in each, and the file's name. The file itself is not stored. Older plans are removed as new ones arrive, and all of them are deleted with your account. See Your data.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Your first flight.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Everything is configured on the window's Settings view. There are no command-line options to learn and no files to edit.

Settings is one page that scrolls, in six sections, in the order a pilot uses them. A row of buttons stays at the top of the page: Your setup, How ATC sounds, X-Plane data, Your account, Appearance and Advanced. A button scrolls to its section, and the section you are looking at is the one marked.

At the bottom, Save and Revert. Save checks every field first. A bad value is highlighted, its section opens, and nothing is saved. With a flight under way, Save reconnects on the same flight with the new settings, waiting for ATC to finish talking first. Save never starts a flight. Revert reloads what was last saved.

docs.title: Your setup
docs.text: What you set on day one: your microphone and speakers, your push-to-talk button, and where X-Plane is.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Setting What it is Use the microphone and speakers Off: no microphone and no sound, for testing Microphone, Speakers / headset Your devices, or System default. A headset switched on after the client started appears after Refresh devices

docs.title: Push-to-talk
docs.text:
The window's button and the Space key always work. Also transmit with adds one more:

Choice What it does Only this window (button, or hold Space) The button, or hold Space while the window has focus A yoke or joystick button, through X-Plane Hold the button to transmit, wherever the focus is

For a yoke or joystick button, press Learn button, then press and release the button you want within 10 seconds. X-Plane must be running. The client reads the button through X-Plane, so anything X-Plane sees as a joystick button works. The client says "Learned button 5 and saved it" (with your button's number), and Button index shows it.

(When you run the client from a console window, there is a third choice, Enter in the console window (toggles). The installed app has no console, so it does not show it.)

docs.title: Phone calls
docs.text:
The last row of this part is Phone calls. Push to talk is the default: on a clearance call you hold the key, as on the radio.

The two Two-way (experimental) choices, Two-way A and Two-way B (two versions of the same thing, being compared), open your microphone for the call: there is no button, you just talk, and ATC answers when you have finished. Use a headset. They are experimental and offered only on some accounts for now. When a flight does not offer one, its choice is greyed and calls stay push to talk. If a two-way call has trouble, it goes on as push to talk and the call screen says "Two-way calling stopped. Hold to talk to continue." The choice applies from your next call; saving it never reconnects the flight.

docs.title: X-Plane
docs.text: Setting What it is X-Plane host and Web API port Where X-Plane's Web API listens. The default, 127.0.0.1 and 8086, is right when the client runs on the same PC as X-Plane End the flight when X-Plane is closed for (s, 0 = never) Seconds. The default is 30. A pause or a stutter never ends a flight. 0 turns it off Silence X-Plane's own ATIS and AWOS during a flight On by default. X-Plane has an ATIS and AWOS of its own on the same frequencies, so with both on you would hear two voices with two sets of weather. During a flight the client switches X-Plane's off and switches it back on when the flight ends. If you had it off already, it stays off

docs.title: App menu (Linux AppImage)
docs.text: Only on Linux, and only when you run the AppImage, there is one more part, App menu, with Add to app menu and Remove from app menu. See Install on Linux. Nowhere else shows it.

docs.title: How ATC sounds
docs.text: Setting Choices ATC voices The voices ATC speaks with. Four choices, in this order: Radio voices: distinct controllers with accents, then under Standard voices: Standard: cheapest, most robotic, Neural: the default and Generative: most natural, about twice neural's cost, may be slightly slower to start. Saving a change reconnects the flight (the same flight), so ATC switches at once; an ATIS already on the air keeps its voice until its next letter ATC delivery How briskly controllers talk: Relaxed, Brisk (the default, about 15% faster) or Fast (about 30% faster). The ATIS is always read at the relaxed pace. Saving a change reconnects the flight (the same flight) Radio effect Clean, Realistic (the default) or Busy day: how much of a VHF radio you hear on ATC's voice Speech recognition How your transmissions are written down for ATC. Two choices: Standard (the default) and Scribe, which knows your flight's names. Saving a change reconnects the flight (the same flight); it applies from your next transmission. If Scribe is not available on a flight, Settings says Scribe is not available on this flight: speech recognition is Standard. See Your data for where the audio goes Hear other traffic on the frequency Client 0.20 prerelease. A checkbox, off by default. On, you hear the AI traffic's calls, and ATC's replies to them, on a frequency one of your radios is tuned to and set to listen to: never over you, nor over ATC talking to you. The row appears only when ATC offers it for your flights, and it matters only on a flight whose Traffic is not None. Saving a change reconnects the flight (the same flight)

docs.title: The radio voices
docs.text: The radio voices are off by default. With them on, each controller on the radio gets a distinct voice with an accent. Within a flight, one frequency keeps one voice. They already sound like a radio, so the Radio effect only adds its key-up click and tail to them. Push-to-talk phone calls, the ATIS and AWOS keep the Neural voices; the experimental two-way call has its own live voice. If the radio voices are not available on a flight, the flight goes on with the standard voices, and Settings says so under the list.

docs.title: X-Plane data
docs.text: Setting What it is X-Plane folder (optional) Leave blank to use the folder X-Plane last ran from. The line under it says "Reading" and the folder the client found, or that it found none FAA procedures and ATC data for X-Plane Installs the FAA's current procedures into your X-Plane, and takes them out again, with Check for update, Install, Update and Remove. See Your X-Plane's data

docs.title: ATC
docs.text: Line What it is ATC address One line, not a field. ATC's address comes with your account when you sign in. The line says From your account. once the client has it, and It comes from your account when you sign in. until then. The window never shows the address itself. If it could not be fetched, the line says so and Try again is beside it This flight While a flight is up, the flight's session id

docs.title: Recording
docs.text: Keep my radio audio to improve SeventyOneTen shows your answer to the recording question, with Allow and Don't allow to change it. Your choice is saved with your account and takes effect at once. Recordings already kept stay until they expire. While it saves, a Saving settings box keeps you from leaving the page until the choice is saved.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
The installed app asks the pilot site for the newest version when it starts, and once a day while it is open. A newer version shows a banner above the views: What changed, Update now and Later. The banner waits until your flight has ended, and nothing is installed during a flight. Update now downloads the new version, checks it, installs it, and the app opens again by itself. On Windows it runs the installer; on Linux it replaces the AppImage file (see Install on Linux); on a Mac it replaces the app, which must be in Applications or another folder you can write to (see Install on a Mac). Later puts that version off until a newer one comes, or until you start the app again.

  • Check now checks on request, and says if it could not.
  • Receive prereleases: early versions, to try before everyone gets them is off unless you turn it on. On, you are offered early versions too. A prerelease is a build for testing; it can have faults, and a later change to the service can stop it working until you update. Turn it on only if you have been asked to.
  • If ATC needs a newer client than yours, the banner says Update required and has no Later.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Setting What it is Theme Night (the default) or Paper. The button at the top right of the window switches it too Show the Approach card: ATC's plan for your vectors and approach, as a diagram On by default. Off, the window never shows ATC's approach plan as a card. The confirmation in the header still shows

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text: Advanced, for developers is folded away unless something in it has been changed. You do not need it to fly. It holds the two sign-in service values that come with the client (change them only when the owner tells you to), Aircraft state from (X-Plane 12 (Web API) is the normal choice; Replay a recording and None, a fixed aircraft parked at Seattle, are for testing without the sim) and a manual source for the X-Plane data pack, for testing.

docs.title: Where things are kept
docs.text:
At the very bottom of the page the window shows the Settings file and the Log file paths, with Open log folder.

What Where (Windows) Settings %LOCALAPPDATA%\xatc-agent-client\settings.json The log file %LOCALAPPDATA%\xatc-agent-client\logs\xatc-agent-client.log Your sign-in Windows Credential Manager, under xatc-agent-client. Never in a file

On a Mac the settings and the log are in ~/Library/Application Support/xatc-agent-client/ (the log in its logs folder), and the sign-in is in your Keychain; Open log folder opens it in Finder. On Linux they are in ~/.config/xatc-agent-client/ (the log in its logs folder), and the sign-in is in your keyring.

The settings file never holds a password or a key. It holds ATC's address (written from your account's answer, never by the window, and never shown in it), the sign-in service's two public values, your SimBrief username or pilot ID, your X-Plane folder, and your last flight plan, which pre-fills the New flight dialog.

The log file rotates at 5 MB and keeps five older files. It has every connect and disconnect, ATC's address, what ATC asked of your X-Plane, and every warning and error. It never has your sign-in or any audio. Send it along when you report a problem.

docs.title: AI traffic
docs.text:
A flight can have other aircraft in it. SeventyOneTen can fill your X-Plane with AI aircraft that depart, taxi, cross runways, fly approaches and land at the airports on your route that have traffic, and ATC works with them: it sequences you with them as with any other aircraft. You read their calls in the log, and you can choose to hear them. This page says how to turn the traffic on, what to install, what the start dialog shows and what you can hear.

A prerelease, for now

The traffic setup shown here is in the client's 0.20 prereleases. The stable client, 0.19.0, does not start AI traffic. The traffic plugin it needs is not on the Download page yet: see What X-Plane needs.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
In the New flight dialog, Traffic chooses how busy the sky is:

Choice What it is None The default: no AI aircraft. The flight is as it always was Light, Typical, Busy, Peak, Saturation From a quiet field to a rush. The airports along your route decide what flies: airliners only where airliners really fly, more light aircraft and business jets at smaller fields Absurd Tests your PC's limit, not realism Custom You choose Aircraft an hour and Filler aircraft

The line under the choice says what it does: "AI aircraft that ATC works around you, their radio calls shown as text in the log."

docs.title: What X-Plane needs
docs.text:
The traffic is drawn inside X-Plane by two things you install once:

  • The SeventyOneTen traffic plugin, which goes in your X-Plane's Resources/plugins folder. Restart X-Plane after you add it. The plugin is not on the Download page yet. Until it is, AI traffic is only for testers who have been given the plugin.
  • Bluebell, a package of aircraft models for X-Plane, which you download yourself. Unpack it into the Custom Data/xatc-traffic/CSL folder of your X-Plane, then start a new flight. When Bluebell is missing, the window shows the folder and a Download Bluebell link.

The window tells you when something is missing. A line under the header says so in words:

  • Traffic is off: the SeventyOneTen traffic plugin isn't answering in X-Plane. The plugin is not installed, or X-Plane was not restarted after you installed it.
  • Bluebell CSL not found: traffic is off. Bluebell is not in the folder above.
  • No traffic on this flight: ATC doesn't offer traffic yet. ATC is not offering traffic on this flight, so the flight goes on without any.
  • No traffic on this flight: there is no traffic at these airports yet. The airports of this flight have no traffic yet, so the flight goes on without any.
  • Another plugin holds X-Plane's AI aircraft: the line names it. Only one can have them at a time, so the traffic yields, for example when you connect to an online network.
  • Traffic is paused while X-Plane is in a menu. It comes back when X-Plane runs again. This is not a fault. It appears when X-Plane is paused or on its Flight Configuration screen.

docs.title: X-Plane's own parked aircraft
docs.text: If X-Plane draws its own parked aircraft, they overlap SeventyOneTen's traffic at the gates. The traffic line then says: "X-Plane's parked aircraft are on; turn off “draw parked aircraft at airports” in Settings › Graphics and restart X-Plane, so they don't overlap SeventyOneTen's traffic." X-Plane saves that setting only when it quits, so the warning goes after the restart. It needs the newest traffic plugin: with an older one there is no warning.

docs.title: Starting a flight with traffic
docs.text:
When Traffic is not None, the start dialog stays open after ATC is ready and shows its progress, so you do not look at an empty sky:

  1. Connecting
  2. Loading airport data
  3. Building traffic, with a line such as "Placing 116 aircraft around KSEA"
  4. Traffic visible

Each step shows its state in words: Done, In progress, Waiting or Skipped. The dialog closes when the aircraft are drawn in X-Plane. It never holds you for good: Fly now closes it at any time, and after 60 seconds it says "Traffic is still starting; you can fly now." With Traffic set to None the dialog closes as soon as ATC is ready.

docs.title: What ATC does with the traffic
docs.text:
ATC works the AI aircraft as it works you, with the same rules:

  • Tower keeps the runway for one aircraft at a time. It cancels an AI takeoff if you enter the runway without a clearance (you are told to "hold in position", then "possible pilot deviation, advise you contact the airport's Tower after landing"; every runway entry without a clearance is recorded as a deviation, except during a declared emergency), clears AI aircraft across runways, and tells you where you stand: you may hear "expect departure delay" when the wait for your runway is unusually long (over about ten minutes).
  • Traffic calls name what matters to you, with the distance: "traffic, Boeing seven thirty seven, two mile final". Tower may add "report traffic in sight".
  • Approach puts you in one landing order with the AI arrivals. You are not given priority: the slower or later aircraft takes the delay, and that can be you, with a slow-down, a longer vector or a "follow". An aircraft closing on a slower one on final is told to cancel its approach, and Tower sends a pair around when the spacing is lost.
  • The AI pilots read back only what is required. Their calls and ATC's replies to them show as text in the log.

docs.title: Hearing the other traffic
docs.text:
By default you read the traffic's calls in the log. You can also hear them. Settings > How ATC sounds has a checkbox, Hear other traffic on the frequency, off by default. It shows only when ATC offers it for your flights, and only matters when your flight has traffic.

  • What you hear: other aircraft's calls, and ATC's replies to them, on a frequency that one of your radios is tuned to and set to listen to. Each AI aircraft has its own voice, and the controller keeps one voice for the position.
  • Never over you: a traffic voice is dropped if you are transmitting, if ATC is talking to you, or if a phone call is ringing or open. One that is playing stops within a tenth of a second when any of those starts.
  • One at a time: traffic voices play one after another, through your radio effect, and an ATIS pauses for them.
  • A limit per flight: when a flight reaches it, the log says "Other traffic's voices stopped for this flight (limit reached); their words still show." and the text goes on.
  • Saving the setting reconnects the flight (the same flight). ATC's words to you keep your ATC voices setting.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Settings lists the setting. Tower says more about how it clears you with traffic about.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the log at the bottom of the window. It says why something did not happen.

If something is simply not built yet, it is on the known limitations page.

docs.title: ATC does not answer
docs.text:
After a transmission with no reply, the log has a No reply line with the reason, in words:

Reason What it means What to do no controller on frequency Nobody works the frequency you transmitted on Check which radio is selected to transmit (TX), and its active frequency. The Frequencies card lists the right ones. On an airport's advisory frequency (advisory · no ATC) silence is normal: the log says "no reply expected" sim paused X-Plane is paused Unpause. ATC is silent and deaf while paused sim in replay X-Plane is in a replay Leave the replay empty transcript The speech recognition heard nothing Check your microphone (below) agent chose silence, readback accepted ATC judged that no reply was needed Normal after a correct readback or a remark. Look for the ✓ Readback accepted busy ATC was still handling your previous call Wait a moment and say it again error Something failed Say it again. If it repeats, send the log file

If ATC answers "Aircraft calling, say again", it did not catch your callsign. Say your full callsign clearly. If you fly under an airline callsign, say it as ATC says it ("Walker seventeen forty-five").

docs.title: I cannot hear ATC
docs.text:
• You hear ATC only on a radio that is tuned to the frequency, switched on, and selected to listen on your audio panel. If the log says a reply was "not played", the line says why: "isn't on COM1/COM2 active" (neither radio was tuned to it), or "COM1 is off", "COM1 isn't selected to listen", "the avionics are off".
  • A call you missed is said again. When the radio can hear it again within about a minute, and you have not transmitted since, ATC repeats its latest call on that frequency once.
  • ATC's audio waits while you are transmitting. Release push-to-talk.
  • Check Settings > Your setup > Audio > Speakers / headset. A headset you switched on after the client started appears after Refresh devices.

docs.title: Cannot transmit
docs.text:
Pressing push-to-talk does nothing, and the log shows an Error line that begins "can't transmit":

The line says What to do the avionics are off Switch the avionics on in X-Plane COM1 is off (or COM2) Switch that radio on. It is the radio selected to transmit, marked TX COM1 isn't selected to listen Select it to listen on your audio panel, or select the other radio to transmit no aircraft state yet (is X-Plane connected?) Start X-Plane: see X-Plane: not connected answer the recording question in the SeventyOneTen window first Choose Allow or Don't allow in the recording question your recording choice is still being saved Wait for the Saving settings box to finish, or choose Try again or Close if it says it could not save

Nothing is sent to ATC when a press is refused.

docs.title: The log shows nothing after "You:"
docs.text:
Your microphone is not reaching the client.

  • Windows Settings > Privacy & security > Microphone: allow desktop apps. On a Mac, open System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone and switch on xatc-agent (it may be listed as SeventyOneTen). On Linux, check your desktop's sound settings and that the microphone is not muted.
  • Settings > Your setup > Audio > Microphone: pick the right device.
  • Push-to-talk releases when the window loses focus. To transmit while X-Plane has focus, use a yoke or joystick button.

docs.title: X-Plane: not connected
docs.text:
• The client and X-Plane must run on the same PC. X-Plane's Web API listens only on 127.0.0.1:8086.
  • Check Settings > Your setup > X-Plane: host 127.0.0.1, port 8086. (Under Advanced, Aircraft state from must be X-Plane 12 (Web API); that is how it ships.)
  • The client keeps looking every few seconds. You do not need to restart it after starting X-Plane.

docs.title: X-Plane too old
docs.text:
The client needs X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer. It uses X-Plane's own Web API, and needs the version of it that arrived in 12.1.4.

The X-Plane pill reads X-Plane: too old, with "X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer is needed; this is 12.1.2" (the version your X-Plane reports), or "X-Plane 12.1.4 or newer is needed; this one is older" when your X-Plane is too old to say which version it is. When X-Plane is connected, the window's header shows its version after the client's.

What to do: update X-Plane 12 to the current release.

docs.title: Tower will not clear me
docs.text:
• Traffic. Tower waits for a departure ahead to be clear, and for an arrival on short final. It tells you why.
  • Wake turbulence. Behind a heavy aircraft or a Boeing 757 the wait is two minutes, behind a super three, and longer from an intersection or an offset parallel runway. Tower says "hold for wake turbulence" and clears you once the time is up.
  • No traffic data. If the client loses X-Plane's traffic feed, Tower holds every takeoff and landing clearance until it is back, because it cannot see the runway. A multiplayer plugin, or another plugin that takes over X-Plane's AI aircraft, can cause this. If the cause is SeventyOneTen's own AI traffic, the traffic line under the window's header says what is wrong.

docs.title: Unable to access data, check connection
docs.text:
A red alert, and X-Plane is paused for you. ATC could not read its airport and procedure data, so it cannot control safely.

  • Check your internet connection.
  • When the data is back, the alert clears by itself and the log says "Data access restored". X-Plane stays paused until you unpause it.

docs.title: Update required
docs.text:
The window shows a banner, Update required.: "This is SeventyOneTen 0.19.0, and 0.20.0 or newer is needed to fly." ATC needs a newer client than yours and has stopped connecting. Press Update now in the banner (it has no Later), or download the newest installer from the pilot site (app.7110atc.com, Download) and run it over your copy. If it says "No update was found yet", press Check again. Then start the client again.

Older than 0.20.0-rc.11: it cannot find updates

The pilot site moved to app.7110atc.com on 2026-10-20. A client older than 0.20.0-rc.11 still asks the old address for updates, so Update now and Check again find nothing. Install the newest version once by hand from app.7110atc.com/#/download; it updates itself from then on.

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text: You see What to do Not signed in Press Sign in. A sign-in lasts 30 days Signed in · offline The sign-in service cannot be reached. Your flight keeps going and the client keeps trying "Your sign-in expires in ..." Press Sign in again whenever it suits you. During a flight, sign in as the same account or the flight will end "Your sign-in has run out. Sign in again to keep flying." Press Sign in again Your passkey is not offered, or is refused Passkeys belong to the sign-in address, which changed on 2026-10-20: add the passkey again. Sign in with your email, password and the authenticator's code, then add the passkey again "This flight belongs to another pilot" You tried to rejoin a flight another account started. Press New flight "Your account isn't allowed to fly" Ask the owner "Can't confirm this flight's pilot right now. Retrying." Nothing to do. The client reconnects by itself and your flight is kept

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
• It opened in my browser instead. On Windows the window needs Edge WebView2, which ships with Windows 10 and 11; on Linux it needs WebKit2GTK; on a Mac it uses the web view that is built into macOS. Without it the same page opens in your default browser and works the same.
  • On Linux I have to sign in every time. Staying signed in needs a keyring (GNOME Keyring or KWallet). Without one, the sign-in lasts only while the app runs.
  • "SeventyOneTen is already running". Only one client runs at a time. Starting it again brings the window that is already open to the front. If the line adds that the window could not be brought forward, look for it in the taskbar.
  • I closed the client mid-flight. Start it again within about ten minutes and choose Rejoin last flight.

docs.title: Flight ended: no ground data from X-Plane for the departure airport
docs.text:
The flight ended at the start. ATC could not get the airport's ground layout (its taxiways, hold lines and stands) from your X-Plane for the departure airport, so it cannot serve the flight. The window's header says Flight ended: no ground data from X-Plane for the departure airport, and the New flight dialog shows what to check:

  • X-Plane has the departure airport's scenery installed and enabled.
  • The client has your X-Plane folder: Settings > X-Plane data > X-Plane folder.
  • X-Plane is running and connected (the X-Plane pill is green), then start a new flight.

An older client (before 0.20.0-rc.17) shows only a general error line for the same end.

docs.title: ATC got stuck on that call
docs.text:
This card is in client 0.20 prereleases; the stable client, 0.19.0, does not show it. A card appears in the window: ATC got stuck on that call. It has been reported. ATC could not make sense of your last call and said nothing. The card has a Reference line, such as "Reference: t-1234", and Close.

  • The flight goes on, and nothing is retried by itself. Close the card and say the call again, in other words if you can.
  • The problem has already been reported. If it keeps happening, send the reference and the time with your report.
  • The technical cause is in the log file, not in the window.

docs.title: The radios will not tune from the window
docs.text: The 1, 2 and ⇄ buttons write to X-Plane. They are greyed out while X-Plane is not connected; hover over them for the reason. Only real VHF COM frequencies are accepted (118.000 to 136.990 MHz).

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text:
Check the known limitations first. Then send the owner:

  1. What you said and what you expected, with the time.
  2. The log file: Settings, at the bottom, Open log folder. It never contains your sign-in or any audio.

docs.title: The window
docs.text: The client runs in its own window, titled SeventyOneTen client, beside X-Plane. It has two views, Radio and Settings. This page is a tour of the Radio view, from the top. Settings has its own page.

docs.title: The header
docs.text:
The top bar has two rows.

  • The name and versions. SeventyOneTen, then the client's version, then X-Plane's version while X-Plane is connected, then the ATC service's version once ATC has welcomed your flight (the window labels that one Gateway, and shows Gateway — until then).
  • The theme button, at the top right: Night and Paper. Its tooltip says which one it switches to.
  • Your flight: callsign (a tail number, or an airline callsign such as "Walker 1745"), aircraft type, departure → destination, and its state (starting, ready, ended). With no flight it says "No flight: press New flight". When a flight ended, the line says why, and the New flight button is highlighted.
  • The approach confirmation: while ATC has you on an approach, a pill beside your callsign shows the kind of approach (ILS, RNAV, Visual), the runway, and ATC is vectoring you. It turns green and says cleared for the approach once ATC clears you. See The approach plan.
  • End flight (only while a flight runs, with a confirmation) and New flight.

Click an airport in the header ("KSEA → KPDX") to open its details.

docs.title: The services row
docs.text:
Three pills show what the client is connected to, beside Radio and Settings, which switch the view:

Pill What it shows Gateway The connection to the ATC service. It reads Gateway: connected, connecting, reconnecting, needs setup, stopped or no flight. Click it for the reason of the last change and Reconnect, which reopens the connection on the same flight X-Plane X-Plane: connected with its version, or not connected. It turns amber and reads X-Plane: paused (or in replay) while the sim is paused: ATC is silent then and does not hear you. X-Plane: too old means it is older than the minimum: see X-Plane too old Sign-in Signed in · your name (green) with Sign out, Not signed in (red) with Sign in, or Signed in · offline (amber) when the sign-in service cannot be reached

When your sign-in is within 24 hours of running out, a line beside the pills says so, with Sign in again. During a flight it asks you to sign in as the same account, or the flight will end.

Under the row, a banner may appear:

  • Lost the connection to the client. Retrying… when the window loses its own client.
  • A setup banner, with Open Settings, when ATC needs something set up or has stopped.
  • The update banner: see Updates.
  • The traffic line (client 0.20 prerelease), on a flight with AI traffic, when the plugin or its aircraft models are missing, the traffic is paused, or X-Plane's own parked aircraft are on.
  • On the Linux AppImage, the offer to add the app to your app menu.

docs.title: The radios
docs.text:
COM1 and COM2, active and standby, exactly as X-Plane has them, with the name of the facility on each frequency when ATC knows it ("Seattle Ground").

  • TX marks the radio selected to transmit on your aircraft's audio panel. It turns red while you transmit.
  • ⇄ swaps active and standby, like the flip-flop key on a real radio.
  • A radio tuned to an ATIS says so: "KSEA ATIS Charlie · looping". An airport's automated weather station (AWOS or ASOS) says its name, and an airport with no tower says "Monmouth CTAF · no ATC": nobody answers on the advisory frequency.

The client changes X-Plane's radios and nothing else, so the window always shows what X-Plane really has.

A radio you hear needs to be on. You hear ATC on a radio only when it is tuned to the frequency, the radio's own switch is on, the avionics are on, and the radio is selected to listen on your aircraft's audio panel. A radio that is off, or not selected to listen, is silent in the window too, and you cannot transmit on it: see Cannot transmit.

docs.title: Push-to-talk
docs.text:
The big button, PUSH TO TALK. Press and hold to transmit (it reads TRANSMITTING), release to stop. Its hint, "Hold, or hold Space", adds the facility you are transmitting to. It works with a mouse or a touch screen, and holding Space does the same while the window has focus. If the window loses focus the button releases, so the radio cannot get stuck keyed.

For a button on your yoke or joystick, see Settings.

docs.title: Read back, and Next
docs.text:
Under push-to-talk:

  • Read back: what ATC is still waiting for you to read back, with how long it has waited. It empties when your readback is accepted.
