  • Next: after a handoff ("contact Portland Approach one two four point three five") it shows Next: Portland Approach 124.350 with COM1 and COM2 buttons. They put the frequency in that radio's standby; then press ⇄. The line goes once COM1 is on it.

docs.title: Last ATC
docs.text: Who spoke last and what they said, with the verdict on your last readback: ✓ Readback accepted or ✗ Corrected. Numbers are shown as you would write them ("119.2"), while the audio says them as a controller does ("one one niner point two"). Under it, a grey line begins "cloud has:" and says what ATC currently knows about your aircraft, for example its stand, whether it is on the ground and the age of the data. It is there so you can see that ATC sees you.

docs.title: The card slot
docs.text:
One card at a time, picked with the chips above it. The slot keeps its height, so the log below never jumps.

Chip When it shows Frequencies Always available: the ATC stations for your flight Approach When ATC starts vectoring you for an approach Parking (with the airport, such as "Parking KPDX") When ATC asks you to say your parking, and on its own when you land or switch to Ground PDC After you request a pre-departure clearance by text. Request PDC is a chip too, while one is possible ⚠ Deviation When ATC flags a pilot deviation, such as taking off without a clearance. It stays until you dismiss it, and the chip stays so that you can bring it back ⚠ No data Unable to access data, check connection: when ATC cannot read its airport data. The client pauses X-Plane; see Troubleshooting ⚠ ATC stuck Client 0.20 prerelease. ATC got stuck on that call. It has been reported. ATC could not answer your last call. The card shows a reference line ("Reference: t-1234") for support, and a Close button. It blocks nothing: the flight goes on and nothing is retried. A card you close stays closed for that call, a later stuck call shows a new one, and a new flight starts with none. The technical cause goes to the log file only ⚠ Flight refused When ATC refuses the flight, for example "This flight belongs to another pilot. Start a new flight." It has New flight and Dismiss

An alert takes the front and its chip turns amber. Hide folds the slot down to its chips.

docs.title: Frequencies
docs.text:
The stations ATC has for your flight, grouped by airport, your departure and destination first. C1 and C2 mark what COM1 and COM2 are tuned to, TX the one you transmit on, and each ATIS shows its current letter.

Each station has two small buttons, 1 and 2: they put its frequency into COM1's or COM2's standby. Then press that radio's ⇄. The list follows the flight: when a clearance or a handoff names another frequency, the card changes with it.

Some rows are special:

  • A tower that is not open around the clock says part-time.
  • An airport with no tower lists its advisory frequency, tagged advisory · no ATC. A call on it is logged as "no reply expected: no controller is on the CTAF", not as a fault.
  • An airport's weather station is a row of its own, tagged automated weather.
  • An airport with no tower and no radio way to Clearance Delivery has a by phone row with a Call button instead of a frequency: see Clearance by phone.

docs.title: Airport details
docs.text: Click an airport name in the header, on the Frequencies card or on the Parking card, and a full-window Airport dialog opens with the airport's facts (towered, or part-time with the hours), its Runways with a diagram, its Frequencies with the same 1 and 2 buttons, and its Procedures: Departures, Arrivals and Approaches. The footer says where each part came from, and Not for navigation.

docs.title: The log
docs.text:
Everything that happened, newest at the bottom:

  • You: what the speech recognition heard, in grey while it is still working. A correct readback gets silence on the radio, so the verdict appears here: a green ✓ Readback accepted or an amber ✗ Corrected.
  • ▶ transmitting on COM1 121.700: the frequency you keyed. On a phone call it says "talking on the phone".
  • ATC: the station, what it said and the frequency. If you were not tuned to it, or its radio was off, the next line says "not played" and why.
  • An ATIS appears in full, once when you tune it and once for each new letter while you stay tuned.
  • No reply: why ATC did not answer. See Troubleshooting.
  • Timing: how long each step of the reply took: "transcript … · agent … · first audio … · total … ms".
  • Flight ended, with the reason.
  • Error, for something the client refused or could not do, such as "can't transmit: COM1 is off".

Scroll up to read something and the log stays where you left it; scroll back to the bottom and it follows again. Clear empties it.

docs.title: Dialogs you will meet
docs.text:
• The startup dialog, each time the client starts: your sign-in, the ATC service and X-Plane. It closes by itself when the first two are ready. After a client restart mid-flight it offers Rejoin last flight.
  • New flight: the flight plan, by hand, from SimBrief or from your account (send a plan), and the Traffic choice (AI traffic); the account tab, the Traffic choice and the start's progress steps are client 0.20 prerelease. It opens by itself when a flight ends, with a line saying why. After Start flight it shows the start's progress; on a flight with traffic it stays up until the aircraft are drawn: Connecting, Loading airport data, Building traffic, Traffic visible, and Fly now closes it at any time.
  • The recording question, the first time you connect: see Your data.
  • The call screen, when you press Call on a phone row: see Clearance by phone.
  • The approach diagram and the parking map, full size, with Bigger.
  • Airport details, above.

docs.title: The approach plan
docs.text: When ATC vectors you for an approach, you fly one heading at a time. The window shows you the whole plan: where ATC means to take you, and where you are on it.

docs.title: The confirmation in the header
docs.text:
While ATC has you on an approach, the top line of the window says so, beside your callsign:

You see It means ILS · RWY 10R · ATC is vectoring you (blue) ATC has a plan for you and is calling each turn. You do not need to ask for vectors ILS · RWY 10R · cleared for the approach (green) ATC has cleared you for the approach

The badge is the kind of approach: ILS, RNAV, Visual, or another kind by its name, such as LOC.

It shows in both views, whatever card is in the card slot.

docs.title: The Approach card
docs.text:
ATC's plan for a vectored ILS, full size: a left downwind, the base turn at 10.8 nm, joining the final at 8.2 nm, outside the final approach fix.

The diagram is drawn course up: the runway is at the top and the final approach course runs down the page.

  • The runway and the extended centerline, with a tick every 5 nm.
  • The final approach fix, with its name (when the data has one) and its distance from the runway.
  • Where you join the final, with its distance.
  • The path ATC plans, as a dotted line: the downwind, the base turn, the turn to final.
  • Your aircraft, turned to its heading.

Beside the diagram:

  • the plan in one line: "ILS RWY 10R · left downwind · base turn 10.8 nm · join 8.2 nm · FAF 4.8 nm" (once ATC has cleared you, the pattern part is dropped),
  • where you are: "You: 5.0 nm out, 3.0 nm left of the final",
  • the airport, the controller and your assigned altitude,
  • the badge: vectors, then cleared.

A prediction, not a clearance

The card shows ATC's plan. It changes as ATC changes it. Fly the headings and altitudes ATC gives you on the radio, not the picture.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Far from the airport, your aircraft sits at the edge of the diagram with its distance, and an arrow points to where it really is. The plan stays large enough to read.
  • Without X-Plane connected, the plan still shows, and the card says your position is not known.
  • As you fly the pattern, the parts behind you drop off, and the dotted line always starts at your aircraft.

docs.title: Bigger
docs.text:
The card slot is small. Bigger opens the diagram in the full window, and Close, Esc or a click outside it closes it again.

If the window is too short for the card's diagram to be readable, the full-size diagram opens by itself when ATC's plan starts. It does so once per approach: after you close it, ATC's updates do not bring it back. Holding Space still transmits while it is open.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
• Close on the card hides it until ATC makes a new plan.
  • Settings > Appearance > Show the Approach card turns the card off for good. The confirmation in the header stays.

docs.title: Your plan in X-Plane's avionics
docs.text:
A prerelease, for now

The plan file first comes with client 0.20.0-rc.16, which is a prerelease: a build for testing, not yet a stable release. Until a stable client carries it, only a prerelease writes the file.

When you start a flight, SeventyOneTen writes your flight plan as a file X-Plane can read, so you can load it into the GNS 530, the G1000 or the FMS without typing the route again.

docs.title: Where it goes
docs.text:
The file is SeventyOneTen.fms, in the Output/FMS plans folder of your X-Plane folder. The client creates the folder if it is missing.

  • It is written each time you press Start flight, whether you typed the plan in or loaded it from SimBrief. It needs a departure and a destination: without both, nothing is written and nothing is logged.
  • The name never changes. Each new flight replaces the file, so nothing piles up in X-Plane's list. If you want to keep a plan, save your own copy under another name.
  • If the log says the file was not written, the file in the folder is an earlier flight's plan. The client leaves the old file as it was; it never empties it.
  • ATC changing your route during the flight does not rewrite it.
  • It is always on. There is no setting to turn it off.

docs.title: Loading it
docs.text: Load it from the aircraft's own GPS, G1000 or FMS, in the cockpit. If the plan does not appear, reopen the flight plan list, or restart X-Plane.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
The file holds your departure and destination airports, your cruise altitude and the route: every fix along each airway, in order. The fixes and their positions come from your own X-Plane's navigation data, so the file matches what your avionics load.

Runways, SIDs, STARs and approaches are not in the file. Choose them in the avionics. A SID or STAR you named in the route is left out too, and the log says so; a plain fix in the route is kept.

docs.title: When something is left out
docs.text:
• A fix X-Plane does not know. If a fix in your route is not in your X-Plane's navigation data, it is left out of the file, and the log says which one, for example "ZZYZX is not in your X-Plane navdata, so it is left out." The client never guesses a position.
  • A very long route. X-Plane's flight plans hold at most 100 waypoints. On a long route the client leaves out some of the fixes along an airway, and the airway still carries the route. If it is still too long, no file is written and the log says why.
  • An airport your X-Plane does not have. The plan starts or ends at the first or last fix X-Plane does know, and the log says so.
  • No X-Plane folder found. No file is written, and the log says so (set the folder in Settings > X-Plane data). Your flight starts anyway.

The log is the one at the bottom of the window, and the line "Your flight plan is in X-Plane as SeventyOneTen.fms" tells you the file was written.

Not checked yet

Whether the G1000 picks up an updated SeventyOneTen.fms without restarting X-Plane has not been checked. If it shows an old plan, reopen the flight plan list, or restart X-Plane.

docs.title: Parking
docs.text: When ATC asks you to "say parking", the window shows what you can answer. It also comes up on its own when you land or switch to Ground.

docs.title: When the card comes up
docs.text:
• When ATC asks "say parking". ATC asks in two places: Approach, at an airport with a large number of airline gates (once, on the check-in or with the approach clearance), and Ground, on your first call after landing when no parking is known (once per taxi-in).
  • When you land. Once you have landed at your destination and slowed to 30 kt or less, the card comes up without being asked. Tower's runway exit does not have to come first, and an airport with no tower works the same way.
  • When you switch to Ground. The card also comes up when the radio you transmit on is tuned to the destination's Ground and is on and listening.

The card comes up once per landing, at whichever of the last two comes first. It does not come up on its own when your parking is already known (you named it), when a card is already up, when it already came up for this landing, or when the airport has no stands. A go-around followed by a new landing is a new landing; a bounce is not.

The Parking card comes to the front of the card slot, titled with the airport, such as "Parking at KPDX". When it came up on its own, a line under the title says "Pick your parking, then tell Ground", and the log says "Landed" or "Switched to Ground" instead of naming a controller who asked. If you close it, it stays closed for that landing; ATC's "say parking" still brings it back.

Needs client 0.20

The card's own line, the log's wording and a closed card staying closed come with client 0.20, which is still a prerelease (the stable release is 0.19.0). On client 0.19.0 the card does not know why it came up: the card appears on landing and on the switch to Ground all the same, but with no line under its title, and the log says that ATC asked for your parking when it did not.

docs.title: What you can say
docs.text:
• Gates and stands, by the names your own scenery gives them, grouped by kind: airline gates, general aviation, cargo, military and the rest. A long group is split into sections by name. An airport with 30 or more stands gets a search box ("Search gates and stands"); it matches every word you type, in any order, so "a 1" finds A1. A very long list says how many more stands are not listed and that you can still say them.

Tap one and the card copies the words to say: "parking gate A1" for a gate, "parking Atlantic Aviation 2" for a named stand. Then say them on the radio. Picking something in the window sends nothing to ATC: you still ask by voice.

The card goes away once ATC has your parking, when the flight ends, or with Close.

docs.title: The parking map
docs.text:
The parking map, opened full size, on demo scenery: the stands that fit a C172, one of them taken, and your own aircraft taxiing in.

Above the lists, the card draws your destination from your own X-Plane scenery:

  • the runways with their numbers and the taxiways with their letters,
  • every stand as an arrow pointing the way the nose goes,
  • your aircraft, when you are at or near the airport.

Stands that take your kind of aircraft (piston, turboprop, jet or heavy jet, as the scenery lists them) are blue. A legend under the map explains the marks: Fits your aircraft, Your choice, Taken, Wrong type and You. Only stands for your type (such as "Only stands for a C172"), on by default, hides the others. If the client does not know your aircraft type it shows every stand and says so. A stand that another aircraft in your X-Plane is sitting on is grey and says taken. You can still pick it, and ATC may tell you it is occupied.

Drag, scroll or pinch to zoom; stand names appear once you are zoomed in. The buttons above the map jump to the ramps that have stands for you. Bigger map opens it in the full window.

Tap a stand, on the map or in the list, and the card shows its name, its kind, whether it is free, and the words to say, with Copy the words.

Everything on the map comes from the X-Plane files on your PC and works offline. If the map cannot be read, the card says "No map" and why, and the lists still work.

docs.title: What Ground does with it
docs.text:
• A parking you name is where the taxi-in ends: a gate or a stand by its name, or a ramp ("Central Ramp" is the stand of that ramp nearest you).
  • Name nothing and Ground asks "say parking" once. If you still name nothing, it taxis you to a general parking and says which. Ground never picks a gate for you.
  • If Ground cannot find what you named, it says so and taxis you to a general parking, named.

docs.title: Pre-departure clearance by text
docs.text: At a busy airport, airline crews often get their IFR clearance as text instead of copying it by voice. You can do the same.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Start your flight. Once ATC is connected, a Request PDC chip shows above the card slot.

  2. Press it. The clearance arrives as the PDC card and in the log:

    N547GA CLRD TO KPDX VIA SUMMA2 THEN AS FILED. MAINT 5000, EXP 16000 10 MIN AFT DEP.
DEP FREQ 119.2. SQUAWK 4521. ATIS K.

  3. Set the squawk and note the departure frequency. There is no voice readback.

  4. When you are ready to taxi, call Ground with the ATIS. You do not need to say "with the PDC".

docs.title: If you cannot get one
docs.text: The card says why, and you call for your clearance by voice (or by phone) instead. Where the airport has no Clearance Delivery, the card names the position that gives it, Ground or Tower. Reasons include: the airport has no control tower (there is never a PDC there), you were already cleared by voice, you are airborne, your flight has no cruise altitude, or a voice amendment is waiting for your readback.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The card is titled "PDC" and the station, such as "PDC · Seattle Clearance", and says "No readback needed. Call Ground with the ATIS when ready to taxi."
  • Press Request PDC again and the clearance is repeated as it now stands, for example after an amendment.
  • Close takes the card out of the slot. The clearance stays in the log.
  • New flight clears it.
  • The chip shows only while a PDC is possible: ATC connected, and no PDC answer already showing.

docs.title: Your X-Plane's data
docs.text: ATC uses the FAA's published data for everything in the air over the US: procedures, fixes, airways, frequencies, tower hours, airspace and minimum altitudes. On the ground, it uses your X-Plane, so that the taxiways and stands ATC names are the ones you see.

docs.title: ATC asks, the client answers
docs.text:
Nothing is uploaded in advance. When ATC needs something only your X-Plane has, it asks, and the client answers over the flight's connection:

What When From The airport's ground layout: taxiways with their names, hold lines, stands, runways as drawn, runway-use rules The departure airport at the start, the destination when you are inbound The scenery pack that wins in your X-Plane, in scenery_packs.ini order Parking stands When the Parking card comes up The same scenery Outside the US only: the airport's runways, frequencies and procedures, the fixes and airways along your route At the start of the flight Your X-Plane's navigation data. It is assumed to be current

It is done safely. ATC can ask only for these kinds of data, for an airport identifier that is checked first, and for a few weather values that X-Plane itself reports, read-only. It can never name a file to read, and it can never write or command anything. (The client itself writes in your X-Plane folder in two places only, listed in Your data.) The log says what was read: "ATC read KBFI's ground layout from your X-Plane".

If X-Plane gives ATC no ground layout for your departure airport, the flight ends at the start, and the window says why (see Troubleshooting). If your scenery has no taxiway data for your destination or a diversion airport, Ground says "taxi to parking at your own discretion". While an answer is still on its way, Ground says "stand by" and calls back.

docs.title: The scenery index, once
docs.text: The first flight after installing reads the header of every airport file in your scenery, once, before it connects to ATC. The New flight dialog shows "Preparing the scenery index (one time)…" with a progress bar. On a slow disk this takes a minute or more. Afterwards only new or changed scenery is read.

docs.title: What the client sends during a flight
docs.text:
About once a second, and at once when you change a radio:

  • your aircraft's position, altitude, speed, heading and whether it is on the ground,
  • your radios: frequencies, which one you transmit on, and whether each is on and selected to listen,
  • your transponder code,
  • the weather at the aircraft (sampled about every five seconds and sent with the once-a-second state),
  • X-Plane's clock, so that ATC judges things like tower opening hours by the sim's time,
  • the other aircraft X-Plane knows about (its AI traffic, SeventyOneTen's own AI traffic when you turned it on, and aircraft a multiplayer plugin adds): the nearest 32.

See Your data for the whole picture.

docs.title: FAA procedures for your X-Plane
docs.text:
Optional. ATC clears you on the FAA's current procedures. If your X-Plane's navigation data is older, your aircraft's FMS may not have a procedure ATC names. Settings > X-Plane data can install the FAA's current procedures into X-Plane, so that the two agree.

  • Check for update shows the release, its AIRAC cycle and its dates.
  • Install downloads it, checks every file, backs up anything it replaces, and writes the FAA's procedure file into your X-Plane's Custom Data folder.
  • Update replaces an installed pack with a newer one.
  • Remove puts your own files back exactly as they were.

You need a flight started to check or install, because the download link comes from ATC. Restart X-Plane afterwards: it reads navigation data only when it starts.

It overrides your navigation data for US procedures

While the pack is installed, X-Plane uses the FAA's procedures in place of your provider's (Navigraph, for example) for the airports it covers. Remove undoes it. Settings warns you when your navigation data is a different AIRAC cycle from the pack: fixes may then not match.

A pack for a cycle that has not started yet can be installed early. Settings marks it Not valid until its first day.

docs.title: What ATC can do
docs.text:
SeventyOneTen staffs every position of an IFR flight. Each controller is on its real frequency, hands you to the next one at the right place, and uses the phraseology of the FAA's controller handbook (JO 7110.65).

Position What it does for you Clearance Delivery Your IFR clearance (from Ground or Tower where an airport has no Clearance Delivery), amendments, a pre-departure clearance by text, and a clearance by phone where there is no radio way Ground Pushback, taxi to the runway, runway crossings, progressive taxi, taxi-in to your parking Tower Line up and wait, takeoff and landing clearances, go-arounds, the runway exit Departure and Center Radar contact, climbs, turns on course, direct routings, descents, holds, diversions, and cancelling IFR (by phone after landing at a field without a tower) Approach The approach to expect, vectors to final (or a direct to a fix at some airports), ILS, RNAV and visual approach clearances

And at every position:

  • Readbacks are checked, and reminded when you forget one.
  • ATIS and weather come from the weather in your X-Plane.
  • Common requests work everywhere: say again, radio checks, questions, emergencies.

docs.title: The rules it plays by
docs.text:
IFR only, for now. VFR departures, pattern work and flight following are not built yet.

Any US airport. Positions, frequencies, procedures, airspace and minimum altitudes come from the FAA's published data. Taxiways and parking stands come from your own X-Plane scenery. Outside the US, ATC asks your X-Plane for the airport's procedures and frequencies too.

Nobody on a frequency, no reply. Tune a frequency no controller uses and you hear nothing. Tune an ATIS frequency and you hear the broadcast.

It will not make things up. Every clearance is checked against the airport's data and your flight before it is spoken. When you ask for something ATC has not been taught, the answer is fixed:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, unable, I have not completed that training."

When the answer is no, ATC says why: "unable, runway one niner not available", "continue holding short, traffic".

ATC calls you first when a real controller would: handoffs, a readback you owe, traffic, drifting off your altitude or your taxi route, a go-around.

One reply per call. Ask for two things in one transmission and you get one reply that covers both.

Silent while paused. While X-Plane is paused or in a replay, ATC says nothing and does not hear you.

Your radio has to be on. You hear a controller only on a radio that is tuned to the frequency, switched on and selected to listen on your audio panel.

docs.title: Not built yet
docs.text:
• VFR: departures, pattern work, flight following.
  • A sidestep to a parallel runway (for now: a go-around).
  • Block altitudes and other less common requests. ATC answers "unable, I have not completed that training".
  • Full emergency handling: vectors to the nearest airport, lost-communication routings. The first steps are there.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: Approach brings you from the arrival to the final approach course and clears you for the approach.

docs.title: Check-in: what to expect
docs.text:
On your first call, Approach gives you the altimeter, your descent, and the approach to expect:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, Portland Approach, radar contact, Portland altimeter three zero zero two, descend and maintain four thousand, expect ILS runway one zero right."

Approach also checks, once, that you have the destination's current ATIS where it has one you can tune: "verify you have information Kilo" if you gave no letter, "information Kilo is current, altimeter three zero zero two" if you gave an old one.

docs.title: Which approach
docs.text:
Approach picks from what the airport publishes for the runway in use: the ILS first, then RNAV (GPS), then a localizer approach. At most airports, in good weather (ceiling 3,000 ft or more and visibility 5 miles or more), it is a visual approach. At a busy airport such as Seattle, the instrument approach stays the plan in good weather: the check-in says "expect the ILS runway one six center", Approach asks once, within 15 nm, "field is at your two o'clock, one two miles, report field in sight", and you get the visual approach when you report the field or the runway in sight. An approach you ask for by name is never replaced.

You can ask for the one you want: "request the RNAV runway one zero right", "request vectors for the ILS". You can also ask for another runway and be vectored for it.

docs.title: Vectors to final
docs.text:
Approach vectors you on a downwind, a base and an intercept heading, as a real controller does for a vectored ILS. You do not need to ask for the next turn: ATC calls each one.

  • The first vector says why you are being vectored: "turn left heading two eight zero, descend and maintain four thousand, vectors for the ILS runway one zero right". ATC does not announce the pattern it plans: the Approach card draws it.
  • Altitudes step down as the minimum altitudes allow.
  • Every heading allows for the wind.
  • Where vectors are not the plan (so far Teterboro, and some RNAV approaches and STARs that end at an initial approach fix), Approach gives you a direct to a fix instead: "after Solberg proceed direct Skuby, descend and maintain three thousand, expect the ILS runway one niner approach", then, before the fix, "maintain three thousand until Skuby, cleared straight-in ILS runway one niner approach". You can ask "request direct Skuby" for a fix of the approach: you get the direct, or one plain reason. Say "unable" and Approach gives you vectors at once, with "cancel approach clearance" first if you were cleared.
  • Coming off a STAR: "depart Battle Ground heading one one zero, descend and maintain five thousand, vectors for the ILS runway one zero right". A STAR that ends on the approach's own fix is cleared at that fix, at least 3 nm before it: "at Shafr, cleared ILS runway two eight right approach".

The window shows this as it happens: the Approach card draws ATC's plan with your aircraft on it, and the top line of the window says ATC is vectoring you.

docs.title: The approach clearance
docs.text:
The last turn comes with the clearance:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, turn left heading two five five, maintain three thousand until established, cleared ILS runway one zero right approach."

Read back the heading, the altitude and the approach with its runway. The altitude and the approach are required; a wrong heading is still corrected. The intercept is 30 degrees or less, at or below the glideslope. At a busy airport a jet is asked to keep 170 knots to the final approach fix.

Approach then hands you to Tower before the final approach fix.

docs.title: Visual approaches
docs.text:
"November five four seven Golf Alpha, field is at your two o'clock, one two miles, report field in sight."

Report the field in sight and you are cleared for the visual approach. If you have not reported it by about 10 nm, Approach gives you the ILS instead. When you report traffic in sight, it may be "number two, follow the Boeing seven thirty seven on a five mile final, cleared visual approach runway one zero right"; when you have not, Approach tells you where you stand: "number two, following a Boeing seven thirty seven on a five mile final". Behind a heavy or a super it adds "caution wake turbulence". Number one says nothing.

docs.title: Sequencing and the missed approach
docs.text:
• Behind other traffic on final, Approach slows you ("reduce speed to one eight zero"), extends your downwind, or holds you.
  • After a go-around, Approach gives you a heading, an altitude and vectors for another approach. You can ask to divert instead.
  • Parking. At an airport with a large number of airline gates (Seattle, for one) Approach may ask you to "say parking", once, on the check-in or with the approach clearance. The window's Parking card shows what you can say.
  • Cancel IFR near the field: "IFR cancellation received, contact Portland Tower".

docs.title: Arriving at a field with no control tower
docs.text: There is no plan and no runway until you name an approach. The check-in gives a descent to the lowest usable altitude and ends "advise you have weather and NOTAMs at the field and advise approach requested". The clearance ends "change to advisory frequency approved, cancel with me, this frequency or on the ground", with nothing to read back, and there is no handoff to Tower. If the approach you ask for is not available, Approach says what is: "unable ILS runway two seven, RNAV runway two seven available, advise approach requested".

docs.title: ATIS and weather
docs.text: ATC's weather is the weather in your X-Plane.

docs.title: The ATIS
docs.text:
Tune an airport's ATIS frequency on COM1 or COM2 and the recording loops, starting mid-broadcast like the real thing. The radio must be on and selected to listen on your audio panel, or you hear nothing. Tune away, or switch the radio off, and it stops. A new letter takes over at the next loop. ATC's calls and your own transmissions come first; the loop picks up again after them.

It gives the information letter, the time, the wind, visibility, the sky, temperature, the altimeter, and the runways and approach in use.

  • The letter starts at a random one and advances when the weather changes enough to matter: the wind turns 10 degrees or changes 5 knots, the altimeter moves 0.02, or the ceiling or visibility crosses a limit (500, 1,000 or 3,000 ft, 1 or 3 miles, and the instrument-condition limits). A change has to hold for a minute, and letters come at least two minutes apart. A change of runway or approach in use, and wind shear starting or stopping, advance it at once. It advances while you are on the ground at the airport (or, for your destination, while the weather estimate can change); in the air the destination's letter holds.
  • Approach in use. At a busy airport in good weather the ATIS names both: "ILS runway one six right approach in use, visual approaches in use."
  • Closing words. "Read back all runway hold short instructions" and "Advise on initial contact you have information Charlie".
  • The sky comes from X-Plane's cloud layers: "few", "scattered", "broken" or "overcast" with the height, and the ceiling named ("ceiling niner hundred overcast").
  • Gusts are reported when the gust is 10 knots or more over the steady wind.
  • Wind shear in your X-Plane weather becomes "wind shear reported", in the ATIS and in Tower's takeoff and landing clearances, when the shear is 10 degrees or more and the steady wind is over 10 knots.

The window names the ATIS on the radio tuned to it ("KSEA ATIS Charlie · looping"), tags each ATIS in the Frequencies card with its current letter, and puts the full text in the log while you listen.

docs.title: The letter on the radio
docs.text:
Say the letter on your first call: "with information Charlie". ATC remembers it for that airport. If you give no letter, the controller asks "verify you have information Charlie"; Tower, checking a departure on the ground, adds the altimeter: "verify you have information Charlie, altimeter three zero zero two". If you give an old one, Approach says "information Kilo is current, altimeter three zero zero two". The "verify you have information" words are also used when the letter changed since another controller had yours. Arriving, Approach checks the destination's letter, once. Departure and Center never ask.

When the letter changes while you are listening to Tower or Approach, that controller tells you on its own, once per letter: "attention all aircraft, information Charlie current", with the cause when there is one, such as a runway change. You answer nothing. It is not said to a pilot who has no letter yet (that pilot is asked at check-in), nor during an emergency.

docs.title: Weather in clearances
docs.text:
• Ground gives the wind and the altimeter with your taxi if you did not report the ATIS.
  • Tower gives the wind with every takeoff and landing clearance.
  • Radar controllers give the altimeter when you check in and when you start down.
  • The runway in use follows the wind. A wind shift can change the runway while you taxi, and Ground then gives you a new route.

docs.title: Weather stations
docs.text: An airport with no ATIS but an automated weather station (AWOS or ASOS) has a broadcast of its own, with no information letter and a new observation each minute: the station's name, "automated weather observation", the time, wind, visibility, sky, temperature and dew point, and the altimeter. A missing element is said as missing. It plays only while a radio on and selected to listen is tuned to it, and only near the airport. The window's radio card names it, and the Frequencies card tags it automated weather.

docs.title: Where the weather comes from
docs.text: The client samples the weather at your aircraft about every five seconds and sends it with its once-a-second state: wind, pressure, temperature, visibility, gusts, wind shear and cloud layers. For an airport you are not at yet, ATC uses X-Plane's regional weather as its estimate. Nothing is fetched from the real world, so ATC always agrees with what you see out of the window.

docs.title: Clearance Delivery
docs.text: Your first call of an IFR flight.

docs.title: The IFR clearance
docs.text:
Call with your callsign, your destination and the ATIS letter. Clearance Delivery reads the clearance in the usual order:

  • the clearance limit (your destination),
  • the route: a SID or radar vectors, "then as filed",
  • the altitude: the initial altitude and the one to expect,
  • the departure frequency,
  • the squawk, different for each flight.

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, cleared to Portland International airport via the Summa Two departure, then as filed, climb and maintain five thousand, expect one six thousand ten minutes after departure, departure frequency one one niner point two, squawk four five two one."

With a SID that has altitude restrictions, the altitude part may instead be "climb via SID", with the expect clause kept. Ask for a SID by name, or for radar vectors ("via radar vectors, Seattle, then as filed"). A SID that does not serve your runway gets "unable, the Summa Two departure is not available from runway one six left". Read all of it back. A correct readback gets "readback correct"; a wrong item is corrected.

You say What happens "Say again the clearance" It is repeated word for word You filed no cruise altitude ATC asks "say requested altitude" before it clears you You filed only your destination as the route ("clearance to Easton") The same as no route: ATC clears you via radar vectors. A destination name at the end of a route is dropped ("PLOOP Easton" is cleared via PLOOP) You filed a SID that serves the runway in use You are cleared on it Your filed route cannot be flown as it is A full route clearance, instead of "then as filed"

docs.title: Where there is no Clearance Delivery
docs.text: At an airport with a Ground frequency but no Clearance Delivery, Ground gives your IFR clearance, in Ground's name, with the same readback. Ask for pushback or taxi first and you get the clearance first; the taxi comes on your next call after you read it back. Where there is only a Tower, the Tower gives it. Call Tower at an airport that has a Ground and no Clearance Delivery and Tower tells you where the clearance is: "clearance on one two one point seven". Where Clearance Delivery exists, Ground sends you there the same way.

docs.title: Amendments
docs.text: When something changes before you depart, Clearance Delivery amends the clearance and says only the items that changed: a new SID, altitude or squawk. Read those back.

docs.title: A clearance by text (PDC)
docs.text: Instead of copying the clearance by voice, press Request PDC in the window. The clearance arrives as text and needs no readback. See Pre-departure clearance by text. There is no PDC at an airport with no control tower.

docs.title: By phone, at a field with no radio way
docs.text:
At an airport with no control tower and no radio way to reach Clearance Delivery (no clearance delivery frequency and no ground communication outlet), the Frequencies card has a Clearance Delivery · by phone row instead of a frequency. You get your clearance by calling.

  1. Press Call. A call screen opens, already calling, with the facility's name like a saved contact. There is no number to dial.
  2. You hear a phone ring, made by the client, from the dial until ATC answers. A normal facility rings once; a busier one, such as the approach control of a busy airport, rings once or twice. ATC answers in the pause after a ring, never in the middle of one, and never after a third ring. If nobody has answered 14 seconds after the dial, the call ends and the log says so.
  3. ATC answers with the facility's name: "Seattle Approach." Ask for your clearance as you would on the radio. The facility is the approach control over the airport, or the Center where no approach control is. It is never Flight Service.
  4. Read the clearance back. A correct readback gets "readback correct, have a safe flight", and the call ends. (When the clearance holds for release, see below.)

To talk, hold Hold to talk on the call screen or your yoke's push-to-talk button. While a call is open, every press talks on the call, not on a radio. ATC is heard whatever COM1 and COM2 are tuned to, with a telephone's sound. Mute stops your side, the keypad is only for looks, and the red button hangs up. (An experimental way to call with no button, offered only on some accounts, is in Settings.)

  • On the ground only. In the air the row says "No phone in flight: use the departure frequency".
  • The row tells you where the clearance stands: "Clearance issued · not read back yet", "Clearance received", then Call back or Call again. If nobody answers, the log says "nobody answered: call again": call again.
  • No text clearance at these fields: ATC does not offer a PDC there.

docs.title: Hold for release
docs.text:
At an airport with no control tower the clearance ends "hold for release, call back when you are number one for departure". This holds at every such airport, whether you reach Clearance by phone or on a radio frequency or ground outlet (then you call back on the radio). Read it back; the call ends with "readback correct, call back when you are number one". The row then reads Hold for release.

When you are number one, press Call for release and tell ATC, with the runway: "number one for departure, runway one six". The release comes on that call, not on the readback of the clearance, and a promise to call does not count as the call. If you do not name your runway, ATC asks "say departure runway". It says when the clearance is void:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, released for departure, clearance void if not off by one seven four three, ... upon entering controlled airspace, proceed direct Helns."

Read it back, with the void time (leave it out and ATC asks once, "read back clearance void time"). The row shows Released for departure · void at 17:43Z. The void time is three minutes after the release. If you are not off by then, the row says Release ran out · call back for a new one.

docs.title: One frequency, one controller
docs.text: At many smaller towered airports, one controller works Clearance Delivery and Ground on the same frequency. There the clearance and the taxi come from the same voice, and you are never told to "contact Ground" on the frequency you are already on. Read back your clearance and add "ready to taxi", and you get "readback correct" and your taxi instructions in one reply.

docs.title: Departure and Center
docs.text: The radar controllers: Departure takes you from the runway into the climb, Center takes you to cruise and back down, and each hands you to the next at the edge of its airspace.

docs.title: Departure
docs.text:
Check in with your altitude. Departure answers "radar contact" with the altimeter and your climb:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, Seattle Departure, radar contact, Seattle altimeter three zero zero two, climb and maintain one five thousand."

Departure climbs you to your filed cruise, up to the top of its own airspace, and Center gives the rest. If your transponder is not on the squawk you were given: "radar contact, reset transponder, squawk zero one seven four", and once more 30 seconds later if it is still wrong.

On a SID with altitude restrictions it is "climb via the Summa Two departure", sometimes "except maintain" an altitude.

On course. After a heading off the runway, Departure turns you toward your route: "turn left heading two niner zero, vectors to Mapel", then "proceed direct Mapel" on its own. A SID that ends on a heading is followed by "proceed direct" its next fix. You can also ask: "request on course".

A route with no fix in it. If your route has no fix ATC knows (none filed, or just your destination's name), the destination stands in for it. Departure says "proceed direct Easton" when it is ahead of you, or "turn left heading one three zero, vectors to Easton" and then "proceed direct Easton" once you have come round. "Request direct Easton" is granted. It is not used within 5 nm of the destination. At a field with no tower the release still says "fly runway heading", and Departure's radar contact adds the direct or the turn.

Still on the wrong frequency? If you call Tower when you should be with Departure: "you're on Seattle Tower, contact Seattle Departure". If you stay on the old frequency, the old controller says "are you with me? contact Seattle Departure one one niner point two", and if you switch but never check in, the new one asks "how do you hear?" The same happens at every handoff.

docs.title: Center
docs.text: The handoff to Center comes on its own: climbing through a thousand feet below the top of Departure's airspace when your cruise is at or above that top, otherwise just before the edge of its airspace, sideways, to whoever owns the airspace there (on a short flight, to the destination's Approach). Check in and Center clears you to your cruise altitude, in steps around traffic if it has to.

docs.title: What you can ask for
docs.text:
You ask for What you get Higher or lower Your altitude, or "unable" with the reason. With no altitude named: "say requested altitude" Direct to a fix "proceed direct Helns", for a fix ahead on your route A heading or a speed Approved when it is safe A deviation around weather "deviation twenty degrees left approved, when able, proceed direct Helns". See A weather deviation A hold "hold west of Battle Ground as published, expect further clearance two one three five" A diversion "cleared to the Olympia airport via direct, maintain ..." To return to your departure airport Radar vectors back, and what to expect To cancel IFR En route: "IFR cancellation received, maintain VFR, squawk VFR, frequency change approved". Near a towered destination it ends "contact Portland Tower" and the frequency; inbound to a field with no tower, "change to advisory frequency approved". Not in Class A airspace (18,000 ft and up): ATC offers the way out, "unable, descend and maintain one seven thousand to exit Class Alpha airspace", and you cancel again below 18,000 ft. Where it cannot give that descent: "unable, IFR cannot be cancelled in Class Alpha airspace". Words that do not say what is cancelled get "confirm cancelling IFR?"

Cancelling IFR in the air is on the radio, as above. After you land at an airport with no control tower, you cancel on the ground: see Cancelling IFR after landing.

ATC never clears you below the minimum altitude for where you are. The FAA's minimum vectoring and minimum IFR altitude charts for the whole US are in its data.

docs.title: A weather deviation
docs.text:
ATC approves a deviation with "when able, proceed direct" and the next fix, and notes that direct. After you have turned away from the direct, the deviation ends by itself, without a call, when you are clearly proceeding direct to that fix again: your heading is within about 5 degrees of the bearing to the fix and has been for about a minute, and you are not drifting away from it. Within 3 nm of the fix it ends at once.

When it is not clear, ATC asks once, "verify you are proceeding direct" and the fix. Answer "proceeding direct" and the deviation ends. If you pass the fix with the deviation still open, ATC asks once about the next fix on your route ("verify you are proceeding direct" that fix), or says "say intentions" when there is no next fix. Coming within 3 nm of the next fix, or being established direct to it, also ends the deviation with no call.

docs.title: The descent
docs.text:
At the top of descent Center starts you down without being asked:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, descend via the Helns Six arrival, Portland altimeter three zero zero two."

or a crossing restriction: "cross Battle Ground at and maintain one one thousand". Asking "request lower" or "request descend via" starts the same descent.

The top of descent allows for speed, so a descent that starts early at high speed is normal. Center then hands you to the next sector, and finally to Approach: at the first of these, once you are inside the destination's approach airspace, 40 nm from the field, or within 2 nm of the arrival's last fix.

docs.title: Cancelling IFR after landing
docs.text:
At an airport with a control tower, your IFR flight plan closes when you land. At one without, you cancel it yourself. Once you have landed at your destination:

  • With no radio way to Clearance Delivery (no clearance delivery frequency, no ground communication outlet), the Frequencies card shows Cancel IFR · by phone under that airport, with Call to cancel and the text "IFR flight plan open · call to cancel". Press it, say "cancel IFR" when ATC answers with the facility's name, and ATC says "IFR cancellation received". The row then reads IFR cancelled. The call works like the clearance call.
  • With a radio way, there is no phone row: cancel on that frequency.
  • If you already cancelled in the air, there is nothing left to cancel and no row.

ATC ends the flight about 30 seconds after the engines are off, call or no call. If that cuts the call before the cancellation is in, the log says the flight ended before it was confirmed. Call before you shut down.

docs.title: The radar controller calls you
docs.text:
• Altitude: 300 ft off your assigned altitude and not correcting, "verify altitude".
  • Course: "verify on course", "verify you are proceeding direct Helns", or a heading back to your route.
  • A missed restriction on a SID or STAR: "verify you are descending via the Helns Six arrival".
  • Low altitude alert: "low altitude alert, check your altitude immediately, the minimum altitude in your area is ...".
  • Traffic: converging aircraft are called in the climb and en route, once each, with the clock position, distance, direction and altitude. A climb held for traffic is answered "unable higher, traffic".
  • Speed: above 250 knots below 10,000 ft, "reduce speed to two five zero knots".
  • A readback you owe for an altitude, a crossing or a procedure, about 30 seconds after ATC stops talking.

docs.title: At every position
docs.text: Things you can say to any controller, and things any controller may say to you.

docs.title: Common requests
docs.text:
You say You get "Say again" The last transmission again "Radio check" As your first call to a position, "Aircraft calling Seattle Ground, read you loud and clear." After that, "November five four seven Golf Alpha, Seattle Ground, read you five" (and once you have spoken on the frequency, the shortened callsign) A question The answer, for: the wind, the weather, the altimeter, the runway to expect, the ATIS, your position, your assigned heading, altitude or squawk, any facility's frequency, the time, a distance, traffic "Thanks for the help", "good day" One short reply, or a "good day" after a handoff

A remark that needs no answer gets none.

docs.title: A call you could not hear
docs.text: Silence is not the end of it. If ATC called you while your radio was off, not selected to listen, or not tuned to the frequency, ATC says its latest call on that frequency again, once, when a radio can hear it again within about a minute, as long as you have not transmitted to that position since. A call lost in a dropped connection is sent again once after the reconnect. The log says "not played" for the call you missed. An ATIS or weather broadcast is not repeated: it loops.

docs.title: Frequency changes
docs.text:
"November five four seven Golf Alpha, contact Seattle Ground one two one point seven."

Reading it back is optional. The window shows Next: Seattle Ground 121.700 with buttons to put it in a radio's standby.

docs.title: Squawk and altimeter
docs.text: Any controller may give you a squawk, "squawk and ident", "ident", or the local altimeter.

docs.title: Traffic and safety alerts
docs.text:
• Traffic advisories: "traffic, two o'clock, five miles, southbound, Boeing seven thirty seven, altitude indicates one thousand feet above you". The traffic is the other aircraft in your X-Plane.
  • Safety alerts: a low altitude alert, or a traffic alert with a suggested escape.
  • A TCAS resolution advisory: tell ATC, and it answers "roger" and issues nothing until you report "clear of conflict".

docs.title: Emergencies
docs.text:
The first steps are built:

  • "Mayday", "Pan-Pan" or squawking 7700: "roger, say fuel remaining and souls on board", and you get priority.
  • Lost communications (7600), or no answer after "are you with me?": "if you hear this transmission, ident". After a handoff, if you are still on the old frequency a minute later, the old controller says "are you with me? contact Seattle Departure one one niner point two". If you are on the new frequency and silent, the new controller says "how do you hear?", and 30 seconds later "if you hear this transmission, ident".

Vectors to the nearest airport and lost-communication routings are not built yet.

docs.title: Pilot deviations
docs.text: When you do something a real controller would report, such as landing or taking off without a clearance, or entering the departure runway without one, ATC tells you on the radio and the window shows a red Pilot deviation alert until you dismiss it. It is there so you notice, and so the flight can be reviewed afterwards. Nobody will ask you to copy a phone number.

docs.title: When the flight ends
docs.text:
ATC ends the flight by itself when:

  • you are parked at your destination stand (stopped within about 60 m of it, with the brake set or the engines off) for a minute, or you have flown and then sit with every engine off for 30 seconds,
  • the aircraft crashed,
  • X-Plane has been closed for 30 seconds,
  • or you press End flight.

After that nothing reconnects until you press New flight.

docs.title: What ATC says when it cannot
docs.text:
• Not possible: "unable", with the reason.
  • Not taught yet: "unable, I have not completed that training". Each of these is logged, so the gaps get filled in the order pilots hit them.

docs.title: Ground
docs.text: Ground moves you between your parking and the runway, on the taxiways of your own X-Plane scenery.

docs.title: Before you taxi
docs.text:
Pushback. Ask for it and Ground approves it, with the direction your tail points: "push back approved, tail south". No readback is needed. If you are IFR and have no clearance yet, Ground sends you for it first ("clearance on one two seven point eight"), or gives it itself where there is no Clearance Delivery: see Clearance Delivery.

Where you are. Ground starts your taxi from where X-Plane says your aircraft is, so a "ready to taxi" call in any words is enough. You can say your position by its name in your scenery ("at alpha eleven", "at the FBO"); if the place you name is far from where your aircraft is, Ground checks: "verify at gate bravo twelve?"

docs.title: Taxi to the runway
docs.text:
"November five four seven Golf Alpha, runway one six left, taxi via Bravo, hold short of runway one six center."

  • The route follows your scenery's real taxiways and names.
  • The taxi instruction ends at the first runway on the way: a hold short of the runway to cross, or of your departure runway. Each later crossing is its own clearance. A hold short for a crossing must be read back; a plain hold short of your departure runway is said, and a wrong runway is still corrected.
  • If you did not report the ATIS, Ground gives you the wind and the altimeter.
  • If X-Plane gives ATC no ground layout for your departure airport, the flight ends at the start and the window says why: see Troubleshooting. At your destination (or a diversion airport) with no taxiway data, Ground says "taxi to parking at your own discretion". While the airport's layout is still being fetched from your X-Plane, Ground says "stand by" and calls back.

Runway crossings are cleared one runway at a time, once the runway is clear: "cross runway one six left at Charlie, hold short of runway one six center". Ground clears each one as you come up to the hold line, without being asked, and you do not need to stop first. While the runway is busy you hear "continue holding short of runway one six center, traffic". A second crossing waits until you have crossed the first, and one asked for from far back is held until you are close.

docs.title: Requests while you taxi
docs.text: You ask for What happens Another runway A new route to it A route "via Alpha" The route goes that way when it can An intersection departure Approved, with the runway distance left Full length A route to the full-length hold line Progressive taxi Ground calls each turn as you come up to it, across the crossings, to the hold line or your parking

docs.title: Ground calls you
docs.text:
• A readback you owe: about 30 seconds after ATC stops talking, "read back hold instructions".
  • Traffic: "hold position, traffic" and the aircraft, "hold for traffic", "follow the Boeing", and "continue taxiing" once the traffic has passed.
  • Off your route: "you are off your cleared taxi route", with a new route from where you are.
  • Moving without a clearance: "hold position" ("hold in position" if you are on a runway).
  • A runway change forced by the wind: a new route and the new ATIS letter.
  • At the runway: "contact Tower" or "monitor Tower".

docs.title: Taxi-in after landing
docs.text:
After Tower sends you to Ground, say where you are parking: a gate, an FBO by name, or "general aviation".

  • Name nothing and Ground asks "say parking" once per taxi-in. If you still name nothing, or name something it cannot find, it taxis you to a general parking and says which. In an emergency it does not ask. The window's Parking card lists the stands you can say, and comes up on its own when you land and when you switch to Ground.
  • A parking Ground cannot find: "unable to find the , taxi to ..." with a general parking, named.
  • A gate that another aircraft is on: you are held on a taxiway until it is free.

docs.title: Readbacks
docs.text: ATC listens to your readback the way a controller does, and the window shows you the verdict.

docs.title: What needs a readback
docs.text:
• An IFR clearance or an amendment: all of its items.
  • Runway instructions: hold short, line up and wait, cleared for takeoff, cleared to land, and each runway crossing.
  • A taxi route's runway, and a hold short whenever it is for crossing a runway. A plain hold short of your departure runway is said but need not be read back, though a wrong runway is still corrected.
  • Altitudes, headings, crossing restrictions, procedures ("descend via"), and an approach clearance with its runway.

A frequency change needs no readback. "Over to Ground", "point seven", or just changing frequency are all fine.

docs.title: A correct readback
docs.text: Silence on the radio, as in real life, and a green ✓ Readback accepted in the window and the log. Only an IFR clearance, an amendment or a diversion clearance gets a spoken "readback correct". On a phone call, a correct readback of the clearance gets "readback correct, have a safe flight" and the call ends (for a clearance that holds for release, "readback correct, call back when you are number one").

docs.title: A wrong readback
docs.text:
ATC corrects the one item that was wrong:

"Negative, squawk six six six two."

When only one item is in doubt, ATC may ask for that item by name: "confirm squawk, rest of readback correct". The correction is spoken firmly, with the wrong item stressed, after a short pause. The window shows an amber ✗ Corrected. A runway hold short that is not your departure runway's must be read back; if you leave it out, ATC asks once for each instruction, "read back hold instructions". (The hold short of your departure runway need not be read back.) After two corrections of the same readback, ATC makes one "verify" and moves on.

A wrong readback of an IFR clearance gets "readback incorrect" and the whole clearance again.

docs.title: What it forgives
docs.text:
Speech recognition is not perfect, and neither is anyone's radio work:

  • Only a clearly different value is corrected. An item the recognition did not catch is not held against you, unless it is a safety item (a hold short, a runway, an altitude), which gets one "read back".
  • Names by sound. "Elma five" for the Elmaa Five arrival, "Helms six" for the Helns Six. The number has to be right.
  • Your callsign as you say it. A filed "WALKER 9798" is "Walker ninety-seven ninety-eight". A call with one character off, or with only the end of your registration, still counts as you. For an airline callsign filed in the New flight dialog, "Walker seventeen forty-five", "Walker one seven four five" and "Walker 1745" all count, but there is no short form: "Walker ninety-eight" alone gets "say again". ATC says a zero in a flight number as "zero" ("American ten zero four").
  • Numbers are strict. A different runway, altitude, heading or squawk is never accepted as close enough.

docs.title: When you forget
docs.text:
About 30 seconds after ATC stops talking, and never while you are transmitting, ATC reminds you: "read back hold instructions", "confirm cleared to land runway one six center". A takeoff clearance is reminded sooner.

The Read back line under push-to-talk shows what ATC is still waiting for, so you can see it before the reminder comes.

docs.title: If ATC did not catch your callsign
docs.text: A garbled call, or a first call to a position with no callsign, gets "Aircraft calling Seattle Ground, say again." It never gets a clearance. A readback without a callsign is fine. (A bare radio check as your first call is the exception: it gets "Aircraft calling Seattle Ground, read you loud and clear." See At every position.)

docs.title: Your callsign, shortened
docs.text: Once you and a position have both spoken on a frequency, ATC shortens a registration to its prefix and the last three characters: "Gulfstream seven golf alpha" (written "Gulfstream 7GA") or "November seven golf alpha". Each new position or frequency starts again with the full callsign, and a new sector with the facility's name. If another aircraft on your frequency has the same three characters anywhere in its spoken identification, ATC keeps the full callsign. You can still say your whole callsign every time.

docs.title: Tower
docs.text: Tower owns the runway: it clears you onto it, off it, and onto it again at the other end of the flight.

docs.title: Departure
docs.text:
Line up and wait when Tower can use the time: never with an arrival close in on your runway.

Takeoff clearance, with the wind (gusts and wind shear when there are any) and where to go after takeoff:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, wind one six zero at eight, runway one six left, cleared for takeoff, fly runway heading."

The runway comes first and sits next to "cleared for takeoff". On radar vectors the clearance then ends with "fly runway heading", or with the turn and the heading ("turn left heading two five zero"). "RNAV to" the first fix, ahead of the runway ("RNAV to Summa, runway one six left, cleared for takeoff"), is said only for simultaneous departures from parallel runways on RNAV SIDs. On a conventional departure, or an RNAV departure on its own, the clearance carries no departure instruction. When there is low level wind shear, Tower adds "low level wind shear advisories in effect". A turn-out or a heading you ask for on a SID cancels it: "cancel departure procedure, fly heading one nine zero, climb and maintain five thousand", and you read both back.

When you have to wait, Tower says why, and clears you without being asked once the reason is gone:

Reason What you hear Traffic on final "hold short of runway one six left, traffic on a two mile final" Wake turbulence: two minutes behind a heavy aircraft or a Boeing 757, three behind a super, longer from an intersection or an offset parallel runway "hold for wake turbulence" An unusually long wait for your runway (over about ten minutes) "hold short of runway one six left, number three for departure, expect departure delay" The runway is occupied Tower holds you, then clears you once it is clear

With an arrival a few miles out, the clearance may be "cleared for takeoff, no delay, traffic on a three mile final". Behind a heavy aircraft it adds "caution wake turbulence". Waiting at the line with an arrival further out, Tower may ask, once per flight, "are you ready for an immediate departure?"

Naming the runway. When you call ready, name your departure runway. If you name another one ("holding short of runway three zero" at runway two five left), Tower says "verify holding short of runway two five left", stressing the runway, and clears nothing until you name the right one. A bare "roger" or "affirm" does not answer it. A second wrong answer gets a second verify, a third "negative, runway two five left".

Your requests: an intersection departure, a turn-out or a heading after takeoff, "need a few minutes". Another runway or full length sends you back to Ground. If Tower cannot, it says "unable" with the reason. If you say "unable" to a line up and wait or an immediate departure, Tower offers an alternative.

After takeoff, once you are airborne and half a mile from the runway in any direction (an early turn included), or at 1,000 ft above the ground at the latest: "contact Seattle Departure".

docs.title: Arrival
docs.text:
Landing clearance, with the wind, your number in the sequence and traffic to follow:

"November five four seven Golf Alpha, wind one seven zero at one zero, runway one six center, cleared to land."

Read back "cleared to land" with the runway. If the runway is not free yet, Tower says "continue" and clears you once it is. Where Tower points out traffic, it may add "report traffic in sight".

Touch-and-go, stop-and-go and low approach. Ask for one on your approach and Tower clears it, in the book's words. Tower clears these only when you ask, and never for the AI aircraft. Read back the operation you were cleared for: a plain landing clearance read back as another operation is caught.

Go-arounds. Tower sends you around when the runway is not clear, and expects one when you call it yourself. You get the missed approach instructions and "contact Approach".

Lined up for the wrong runway on final? "Confirm you are lined up for runway one six center." Close in, it is a go-around: "go around, not lined up for the assigned runway".

The runway exit and Ground. Where your exit leads to another runway, or your parking is across the runway, Tower calls the exit on the rollout in one transmission with the handoff: "turn left at Mike, hold short of runway one six left, contact Seattle Ground one two one point seven". Read back the hold short and the frequency. At other exits there is no rollout call: once you are past the hold line, Tower says "contact Seattle Ground" and the frequency.

docs.title: Tower calls you
docs.text:
• A takeoff or landing readback you owe: "confirm cleared for takeoff runway one six left".
  • Rolling without a clearance: "stop immediately, I say again, stop immediately, you are not cleared for takeoff".
  • A cancelled takeoff: at low speed "cancel takeoff clearance" with the reason; faster, "stop immediately".
  • A possible pilot deviation, when you landed or took off without a clearance, took off without reading back the takeoff clearance, or entered the departure runway without a clearance: "possible pilot deviation, advise you contact Seattle Tower after landing". The window shows a red alert. It is not given at a field with no control tower.

docs.title: What Tower knows about traffic
docs.text: Tower clears takeoffs and landings against the other aircraft in your X-Plane: SeventyOneTen's own AI traffic, X-Plane's AI traffic and aircraft a multiplayer plugin adds. A runway with a departure still on it, or an arrival on short final, is not yours yet. If X-Plane's traffic goes missing or stale, Tower holds every takeoff and landing clearance ("holding due to temporary traffic feed failure") until it is back. Closely spaced parallel runways are treated as one runway for wake turbulence.
